For a datetime-ordered queryset this class must derive from/replicate `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member can be None, causing an AttributeError 500

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member`, which is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is `None` for requesters who are not org members (e.g. org auth token / integration token authenticated requests, or staff access without membership). false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims negative cursor offsets are a supported feature, which they are not

The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" for "efficient reverse pagination". Nothing in `Cursor` was changed, and the rest of the codebase explicitly rejects negative offsets (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator` all raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) while Django querysets raise `ValueError` on negative slices. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a validated, supported input.

Eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans with no metric or log

The new trimming logic hardcodes `span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000`, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) which is now never used, so the limit is neither configurable nor consistent with the Python config. In addition, the previous behaviour emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and an error log when a segment exceeded the span count; now spans are dropped silently inside Lua, so there is no metric, log, or dashboard signal that data loss occurred. Please make the limit a script argument driven by `max_segment_spans` and return/emit an eviction count so the loss is observable.

Module docstring still describes plain sets and omits insert-time eviction

The module docstring (steps 2-3 around line 38-39 and the glossary entry on line 58: "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes the span buffers as Redis sets and says the payload is added "to the set". They are now sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are evicted (oldest-first) once a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Since this docstring is the primary explanation of the buffer's Redis layout, it should document the new type and the lossy eviction behaviour.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit-log code path have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (~90 new lines, including a dedicated negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests at all. Basic coverage would have caught that `get_item_key` cannot handle the `datetime` field the endpoint orders by and that negative slice starts raise `ValueError` in Django. At minimum there should be tests for: the paginator with the endpoint's actual order_by, the permission gate (member=None, non-superuser, non-privileged member), and the rejection of negative offsets.

No test for the new insert-time eviction, the headline change of this PR

All changes to `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`. Nothing exercises the new behaviour: no test pushes more than 1000 spans into a segment to verify that `zpopmin` trims to the limit, that the lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` spans are the ones evicted, that the root/segment span survives, or that merging two over-limit sub-segments via `zunionstore` still trims correctly. The eviction path (and the score-based ordering it depends on) is therefore completely untested.

Redirect-resolution loop limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000 and its warning comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. This 10x reduction means segment trees deeper than ~1000 redirects now stop resolving and get split into separate segments, which is a user-visible behaviour change unrelated to the stated purpose of this PR (insert-time eviction). Either keep the previous bound or document the new limit and the reason for lowering it.

Redis value type change from SET to ZSET on the same key prefix breaks in-flight segments

`span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` keys are switched from plain Redis SETs (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`/`scard`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`/`zcard`) while keeping the exact same key names. Keys written by the previous code version live for `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), and during a rolling deploy old and new consumers write to the same keys. Any `ZADD`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZSCAN` against a key that is still a SET returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, which raises out of the pipeline in `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` and will crash-loop the consumer (or permanently fail those batches) until every legacy key expires. The key prefix needs to be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) or the data explicitly migrated/flushed as part of the rollout.

Superuser check uses request.user.is_superuser instead of is_active_superuser(request)

The gate for the new pagination mode uses the raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag. In Sentry, holding the superuser flag is not the same as having an elevated/active superuser session; the supported check is `sentry.auth.superuser.is_active_superuser(request)` (or staff equivalent). Using the raw flag grants the privileged code path to any account with the flag set regardless of whether superuser mode was activated, bypassing the elevation requirement that the rest of the codebase enforces. Note also that `has_global_access` is true for every member of an open-membership organization, so the "authorized administrators" framing in the comment does not match what is actually checked.

Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can hard-fail a whole batch

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing while neighbouring optional fields use `val.get(...)`. Any message lacking the field (older producers, replayed/spillover topics, malformed payloads) raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the entire arroyo batch rather than a single message and will crash-loop the consumer on a poison message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly invalidating the single span.

max_segment_spans config is now dead code

`self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` is still set in `SpansBuffer.__init__` (default 1001) but the only consumer of it — the span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` — was deleted, and the new limit is hardcoded as `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect. Either thread the value into the Lua script as an ARGV or remove the constructor parameter.

zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting span scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the identical span payload is a member of both source sorted sets — which happens with at-least-once Kafka redelivery where the same payload was first buffered under the parent key and later under the redirect-resolved set key — the resulting score becomes the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values (~2x epoch seconds). That span then sorts as the "newest" member forever, so the new `zpopmin` eviction will evict legitimate recent spans instead, and the score is no longer a meaningful timestamp. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cross-request cache of allowlist eligibility is stale, never invalidated, and keyed by `hash()`

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the allowlist decision in the shared cache for 60s under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))}`. Three problems: (1) the option value `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` is not part of the key and `invalidate_upsampling_cache()` is dead code (no caller anywhere in this PR), so after an operator changes the allowlist—including turning it off because counts are wrong—requests keep returning 10x-inflated or non-upsampled counts for up to 60s with no way to flush; (2) `options.get` is already backed by an option cache, so this adds a correctness window for no measurable gain; (3) using `hash()` of the project-id tuple makes different project sets collide into the same key, which silently applies the wrong upsampling decision (use a deterministic, collision-free key such as the sorted ids joined by commas).

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is computed from the outer `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` actually queried

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first parameter and executes the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (`discover` for the errors-only probe, `scoped_dataset` for the original), so the transform decision can be made for the wrong dataset: e.g. the errors-only probe against `discover` is evaluated with `dataset == metrics_enhanced_performance` (never upsampled), and conversely a query executed against a non-error dataset can be evaluated as `discover`. The result is counts that are inconsistently upsampled (or a transform sent to a dataset lacking `upsampled_count`). Pass `scoped_dataset` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, hiding mis-set sample rates

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`, and invalid/zero values are dropped by the `if client_sample_rate:` guard. If a test supplies a malformed `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, `sample_rate` is silently not set and the stored event gets `sample_weight = 1`; the upsampling assertions (e.g. `count == 10`) then fail with no indication of why. Let the conversion raise (or assert) so test authors get an actionable error instead of a mysterious count mismatch.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly a local workspace artifact: it makes `git submodule update`/`git clone --recurse-submodules` fail or warn about an uninitialized submodule with no URL, and pollutes the repo tree. It must be removed before merging.

Error-focus detection reads the raw request query instead of the query actually executed

`_is_error_focused_query()` inspects `request.GET["query"]`, but the query string that is actually executed is passed into `_get_event_stats` as the `query` argument and can differ from the request parameter. In the dashboard split path the endpoint builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (error-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transaction-only); both are evaluated using the same unmodified `request.GET["query"]`. So an error-only split query will not be upsampled unless the user happened to type `event.type:error`, and a transaction-only split query *will* be upsampled if the user's original query contained `event.type:error`, summing `sample_weight` over transactions where the column does not exist. The detection should operate on the query string handed to the dataset, not on the request parameter.

New file violates the repo's formatting rules (will fail lint/CI)

`pyproject.toml` configures black/flake8 with `line-length = 100`, but the `cache_key` assignment on this line is ~110 characters, and the new file plus the edits in `organization_events_stats.py` contain trailing whitespace on several blank/comment lines (e.g. after `should_upsample = ...` and inside the docstrings). Pre-commit/black and flake8 will reject the diff as-is; run the formatter before merging.

No test covers the public entry point or its caching behaviour

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — the only function the endpoint actually calls, and the one containing the new 60s shared-cache logic — is never tested, nor is `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. As a result, the cache-hit path (including the `cached_result is not None` handling of a cached `False`, and the key-building logic duplicated between the two functions) is unverified, and regressions in the caching layer would silently change query results in production.

`sum(sample_weight)` silently returns 0 for events without a sample weight

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count()`, which is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. The docstring asserts "we rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists", but a project only gets a `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` once the SDK sends `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`; events ingested before upsampling was enabled, events from SDKs that do not send it, and events from other event sources in the same (allowlisted) project will have a NULL/0 weight. For those rows `sum(sample_weight)` contributes 0 instead of 1, so adding a project to the allowlist silently zeroes or undercounts historical and non-instrumented error counts in charts and alerts. The aggregate should fall back to 1 per row when `sample_weight` is absent (e.g. `sum(if(sample_weight > 0, sample_weight, 1))` or an equivalent coalesce).

`upsampled_count` is exposed as a public discover function

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any API consumer can request `field=upsampled_count()`/`yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover/transaction queries. Since it compiles to `sum(sample_weight)` and `sample_weight` does not exist for transaction rows, this is a user-reachable path to a raw Snuba/ClickHouse "unknown column" error (500/snuba error surfaced to the client), and it becomes an unintentionally supported public API surface. Also, the aggregate returns `toInt64(...)` but declares `default_result_type="number"`; `"integer"` matches the actual value type and the result type reported for `count()`.

`upsampled_count` is only registered for the discover dataset but is applied to the errors dataset

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter` in `discover.py`. However `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform()` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is errors`, so for `?dataset=errors` requests the endpoint will send `upsampled_count() as count` to a builder backed by `ErrorsDatasetConfig`, which maintains its own independent `function_converter`. If that config does not also register `upsampled_count`, every errors-dataset timeseries request from an allowlisted project will fail with `InvalidSearchQuery: upsampled_count() is not a valid function` (HTTP 400) instead of returning data. Either register the function for the errors dataset config too, or restrict the transform to datasets that actually expose it. Note that the added tests only exercise the default (discover) dataset, so this path is completely uncovered.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error IDs with nodestore values by dict order

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns its results in the same order as the input list and includes an entry for every requested node id. That is only true for the naive dict-comprehension backend; other backends (e.g. Bigtable, which returns rows in row-key order, and caches that skip misses) can return a differently ordered and/or shorter mapping. The result is `ErrorEvent.id` values attached to the wrong event payload, and silently dropped/mismatched errors. Iterate over `node_ids`/`error_ids` and look the data up by node id instead (`events.get(node_id)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders a hard-coded empty table

When `organization.features.includes('use-table-widget-visualization')` is true, the widget table is rendered as `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`. The actual query result (`result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, title, loading state, custom field renderers) is never passed through, and because `columns` is `[]` (not nullish) the component's fallback to derive columns from `tableData.meta.fields` is also bypassed. Any organization that gets this flag will see completely blank table widgets instead of their data. Either wire the real `result`/`fields` into the new component or keep the branch out of the released code path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics recorded before the feature check and payload validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs at the top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature gate and before schema validation. Every probe/404 and every malformed request is therefore counted as an assemble call, which makes the metric unusable for measuring real usage. Move the record after the feature check (and ideally after validation succeeds).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity chunk, silently skipping identities

`check_auth_identities` processes up to `chunk_size=100` identities serially, each performing an external IdP `refresh_identity` network call, under the new `processing_deadline_duration=60`. That is a ~0.6s budget per identity. If the deadline is hit the task is killed, but `check_auth` has already bumped `last_synced` for the whole batch, so the unprocessed identities will not be re-selected until the next ~24h cutoff and their SSO validity silently goes unchecked. Either raise the deadline, lower the default chunk size, or only update `last_synced` after an identity is actually processed.

Custom cell renderers returning falsy nodes are silently replaced by the default renderer

`TableWidgetVisualization`'s prop docs (and the story) state that returning `undefined` from `renderTableBodyCell`/`renderTableHeadCell` falls back to the default renderer, but the implementation checks `if (cell)`. A custom renderer that legitimately returns `null`, `''`, `0` or `false` (e.g. to render an intentionally blank cell) will be overridden by the default field renderer. Check explicitly for `undefined` (`if (cell !== undefined)`).

Error context silently empty for replays older than the default stats period

`self.get_filter_params(request, project)` falls back to the default stats period (14 days) when the caller doesn't pass `statsPeriod`/`start`/`end`, and those bounds are used for the `query_replay_instance` lookup that produces `error_ids`. For a replay older than the default window the Snuba query returns nothing, `error_ids` is empty, and the summary is generated without any error context with no indication to the caller. Derive the time range from the replay itself (or require explicit bounds and return an error when the replay isn't found).

Error/breadcrumb interleaving compares seconds against milliseconds

`gen_request_data` orders errors relative to replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data, which is a Unix timestamp in seconds (~1.7e9), while rrweb recording events carry `timestamp` as epoch milliseconds (~1.7e12). Every error will therefore compare as "earlier" than every breadcrumb and all error log lines will be emitted before any breadcrumb, destroying the chronological context the feature is built to provide. The new tests don't catch this because the fixtures build segment events with second-resolution timestamps; please normalize units (and add a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps).

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter is skipped unless a search query is typed

`sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `searchQuery` is empty, and only applies the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` filter in the search branch. As a result `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown in the attributes tree by default and disappear only while the user is searching — the opposite of the intent, and visibly inconsistent behavior. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied to the base list before the search short-circuit.

Header alignment is derived from the display name instead of the column key

`fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType)` passes the human-readable column label. When a caller supplies custom display names without an explicit `type` (the documented use case — e.g. `{key: 'count(span.duration)', name: 'Count of Span Duration'}` in the spec fixture), `fieldAlignment` falls back to name-based detection and cannot recognize the aggregate/numeric field, so numeric columns are left-aligned. Use `column.key` for the field argument.

Merged-PR comment template's trailing newline produces blank lines between issues

`MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE` now ends with `
`, while both GitHub and GitLab build the list with `"
".join(...)`. The rendered comment therefore has a blank line between every issue and an extra blank line before the trailing `<sub>Did you find this useful?...</sub>` footer (visible in the updated test expectations as `


<sub>`). Drop the trailing newline from the template (or join with `""`) so the bullet list renders as a compact list.

No-op migration comments point to a migration that isn't in this change

Both 0917 and 0920 are gutted to `return` with the comment "See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration." No such migration is added in this PR, so unless 0921 already exists on the base branch the comment is a dangling reference and a future reader cannot find the replacement migration. Please land the referenced migration together with these no-ops or fix the pointer.

One nonconforming report causes the entire batch to be dropped with 422

The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails, so all other (valid) reports in the same POST are discarded and never counted. This is risky for a data-collection endpoint: the serializer requires `destination` and `attempts` (fields the Reporting API spec does not include in the delivered payload — browsers send `age`/`type`/`url`/`user_agent`/`body`) and restricts `type` to a fixed `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES` choice list, so newly introduced or spec-variant report types will now fail hard instead of being measured. Prefer validating per report and skipping/counting invalid ones (with a metric/log) while still returning 200 for the rest.

`Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` guard is always true

`normalizeDateTimeParams(selection.datetime)` always returns an object, so `Boolean(normalizedDateRange)` is unconditionally `true` and the `enabled` option is effectively just the feature-flag check. If the intent was to avoid firing the request before page filters are ready, the guard needs to inspect an actual field (e.g. `statsPeriod`/`start`/`end`) or use `usePageFilters().isReady`; otherwise drop the dead condition.

get_environment_info issues a Snuba + DB query per issue inside comment generation

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba event lookup) followed by `event.get_environment()` (a DB/environment lookup) for every issue, and both GitHub and GitLab `get_comment_body` call it once per issue in a list comprehension. That adds up to 5 extra Snuba queries plus environment fetches per PR/MR comment, on a path that previously only used already-loaded `Group` fields. Consider resolving the environment in bulk (or from data already available on the group) instead of per-issue, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment, so these failures would be hard to notice.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code invalidation is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The code decrypts the whole `backupCodes` array, nulls out the used index and writes the whole array back with `prisma.user.update`. Two requests presenting the *same* backup code concurrently can both pass the `indexOf` check before either update lands, so a single backup code can be consumed more than once (defeating the "each code can be used exactly once" guarantee stated in `backup_code_instructions`). Likewise, two concurrent logins using *different* codes will each write a snapshot taken before the other's update, so one consumption is silently lost and that code becomes reusable. This needs to be done in a transaction with a conditional update (or by storing codes as individual rows / hashed values that can be deleted atomically).

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code blob URL is never revoked when the modal closes

`URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is only revoked when a new setup run creates another URL (line 98). `resetState()` and unmounting do not revoke it, so the blob containing the plaintext backup codes stays alive for the lifetime of the document and remains fetchable from its `blob:` URL after the dialog is closed. Revoke the URL in `resetState()` and in a cleanup effect on unmount.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Assertion on isChecked() always passes, FIXME left in place

`await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise object, which is always truthy, so this step can never fail — exactly as the newly added FIXME comment says. Since the correct form is already used in the sibling test (`[data-state="checked"]` locator) or `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()`, fix the assertion rather than documenting it; as-is the first test silently stops verifying that 2FA was actually enabled.

Backup code login can bypass the password check entirely

In `authorize()` the password is only verified when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch is evaluated afterwards and takes precedence over the TOTP branch whenever `credentials.backupCode` is non-empty. An attacker who posts `email` + any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") + a valid `backupCode` therefore skips password verification completely and is logged in on the strength of the backup code alone. Backup codes are long-lived static strings that users are encouraged to download to a text file (`cal-backup-codes.txt`), so this turns a comparatively weakly-protected artefact into a full single-factor account takeover. The backup-code branch must require a successful password verification for CAL-identity users (or the password check must not be skippable by merely supplying a totpCode).

Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed

`setup.ts` stores the backup codes with `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` and the login path decrypts them to compare. Unlike `twoFactorSecret`, backup codes never need to be recovered in plaintext after they are shown once, so they should be hashed (e.g. bcrypt/argon2, as passwords are) and compared by hash. As written, anyone with read access to the `users` table plus the encryption key (a single env var shared across the deployment) obtains working second factors for every 2FA user, and combined with the password-bypass issue in this same function that is sufficient for account takeover.

No test covers the security-critical backup code verification paths

The only new coverage is the download/copy/close buttons of the backup-code dialog. The actual new logic — logging in with a backup code, rejecting an incorrect code, the single-use invalidation in `next-auth-options.ts`, and disabling 2FA with a backup code in `totp/disable.ts` — is completely untested (the PR itself notes this as a TODO). Given that these paths grant account access and mutate the stored code list, at least a happy-path login-with-backup-code test plus a replay test (same code rejected the second time) should be added before merge.

Submitting an empty backup code gives the user no feedback

The login form is rendered with `noValidate`, so the `required`/`minLength` attributes on the backup-code input are not enforced, and the zod schema only validates `email`/`password` (everything else is `passthrough`). Submitting the backup-code step with an empty field sends `backupCode: ""`, the server falls through to the TOTP branch and returns `SecondFactorRequired`, which this handler maps to `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` without setting an error message. The result is a submit that appears to do nothing. Validate the backup-code field client-side (or surface an error for `SecondFactorRequired` while in backup-code mode).

Unvalidated request body can crash the disable endpoint

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` assumes the field is a string; posting `{"backupCode": 1}` or `{"backupCode": []}` throws `replaceAll is not a function`, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throws on any corrupt/legacy ciphertext. Both throw out of the handler and surface as an unhandled 500 (with a stack trace in logs) instead of a controlled 400. Validate the body (e.g. with zod) and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning `ErrorCode.InternalServerError`.

missing_backup_codes message points users to a settings page that cannot generate codes

"No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown to any user whose `backupCodes` column is null — which is every user who enabled 2FA before this migration, since there is no backfill. There is no UI anywhere in this PR that generates backup codes for an already-enabled 2FA account; the only way to obtain codes is to disable and re-enable 2FA. The message therefore instructs users to perform an action that does not exist. Either add a regenerate action or change the text to describe the actual recovery path.

onEnable() is now only called from the Close button, leaving UI state stale if the dialog is dismissed

Previously `onEnable()` fired immediately after the enable API returned 200. Now it is only invoked by the `backup-codes-close` button. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (X button, Escape, overlay click → `onOpenChange`), 2FA is already enabled server-side but the parent never learns about it, so the two-factor switch keeps showing "off" until a page reload. Worse, `resetState()` is also skipped in that path, so `step` stays at `DisplayBackupCodes` and `backupCodes` keeps the old values: reopening the modal immediately shows the previous user's/previous run's backup codes instead of starting at the password step. Reset state and notify the parent from `onOpenChange` as well.

tabIndex={-1} makes the password show/hide toggle keyboard-inaccessible

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the reveal button removes it from the tab order for every `PasswordField` in the app, not just the 2FA modals. `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []` is used for the calendar id in `createEvent`, `createAttendees`, `updateEvent` and `deleteEvent`. Since `EventManager` now invokes these once per destination calendar with the corresponding host's credential, every host's run targets the first host's calendar id, producing duplicate events on the main host's calendar (or API errors) and no event on the other hosts' calendars.

No tests for the new multi-destination calendar fan-out

`createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` now loop over an array of destination calendars, fetch foreign credentials from the DB and build one reference per created event, and every provider service was touched. The only test change in the PR is flipping one e2e expectation from `null` to `[]`. There is no unit/integration coverage asserting that a collective event with two hosts creates exactly one event per host calendar, that references carry the right `credentialId`/`externalCalendarId`, or that the single-host fallback is unchanged — all of which the findings above show are currently broken for several providers.

Office365 createEvent always uses the first host's calendar id

Only `destinationCalendar[0]` is honoured. With the new multi-destination flow, `EventManager` calls `createEvent` once per destination using that destination's owner credential; for the second host this builds `/me/calendars/<first host's calendar id>/events` while authenticating as the second host, which 404s (or writes to the wrong calendar if ids happen to collide). true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"

When the parsed response has no `refresh_token`, the helper injects the literal string `"refresh_token"`. This value is then written to the DB by callers that merge the parse result into the stored key — e.g. `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `{...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}` and `zoomvideo` does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`. Microsoft's refresh response legitimately may omit `refresh_token` (the schema marks it `optional()`), in which case the previously valid refresh token is destroyed and the credential can never be refreshed again — the user must re-install the app. The dummy value should never be persisted; preserve the existing refresh token instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema is built from invalid computed keys and strips all other fields

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not produce dynamic key matchers: `ZodString.toString()` yields the string "[object Object]", so both computed properties collapse into a single literal key `"[object Object]"` (the second definition overwriting the first). The schema therefore only validates `{ access_token: string }`, the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" rule is never applied, and — because zod objects strip unknown keys — every other field of the sync-endpoint response (expiry/expiry_date, refresh_token, instance_url, api_domain, scope, token_type) is dropped from `data`. Downstream this corrupts stored credentials, e.g. zoomvideo sets `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` → `NaN`, office365 never updates its expiry, and salesforce persists a key without `instance_url`. Use `.passthrough()` plus an explicit expiry field, or validate per-app.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google credential key is overwritten with a zod safeParse result object

`parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns a zod `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed credential. The old code was `const key = googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which returned the keys themselves. Now `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` persists `{"success":true,"data":{...}}` as the credential key. After the first access-token refresh, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth()` will fail and the user's Google Calendar integration is permanently broken until they reconnect. Either return `.data` from the helper or use `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` here.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync path returns a raw fetch Response while several callers expect axios/googleapis shapes

In the credential-sharing branch the helper returns the `Response` object from `fetch`. Callers do not all consume a `Response`: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` reads `res?.data` (googleapis style), `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios style), `hubspot` reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (already-parsed object), and `larkcalendar` passes it to `handleLarkError` which expects the Lark `{code, data}` envelope. With syncing enabled these paths throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` or silently compute `NaN` expiries, i.e. credential sync simply cannot work for those apps. The helper needs a single, documented return contract (e.g. always return parsed JSON) and the call sites must be adapted.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

Sync path returns a raw fetch Response while several callers expect axios/googleapis shapes

In the credential-sharing branch the helper returns the `Response` object from `fetch`. Callers do not all consume a `Response`: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` reads `res?.data` (googleapis style), `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios style), `hubspot` reads `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` (already-parsed object), and `larkcalendar` passes it to `handleLarkError` which expects the Lark `{code, data}` envelope. With syncing enabled these paths throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` or silently compute `NaN` expiries, i.e. credential sync simply cannot work for those apps. The helper needs a single, documented return contract (e.g. always return parsed JSON) and the call sites must be adapted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId

`refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Here the credential's primary key is passed instead of `credential.userId`, so with credential sharing enabled Cal.com asks the self-hosted endpoint for the tokens of a completely different (or non-existent) user, which at best fails and at worst installs another user's tokens on this credential. `refreshAccessToken` needs the userId plumbed through.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Token refresh failure detected via `response.statusText !== "OK"`

Checking `statusText` is unreliable (it is empty for HTTP/2 responses and may differ per server), so a successful refresh can be rejected while the error message surfaced to the user is an empty string. Use `if (!response.ok)` and include the response body in the thrown error for diagnosability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce refreshes the token on every request but then connects with the old access token

`getClient()` now unconditionally performs a `refresh_token` exchange on every instantiation of the service (no expiry check), yet the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with `credentialKey.access_token` / `credentialKey.instance_url` from the stale credential rather than the freshly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data`. The refresh therefore adds a blocking round trip (and Salesforce token-request rate-limit pressure) on every booking while not actually fixing an expired token. Use the newly returned `access_token`/`instance_url`, and only refresh when the stored token is expired.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook handler has no method guard and throws unhandled errors on bad input

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` for a malformed/absent body (e.g. any GET to this route), and `symmetricDecrypt` / `JSON.parse` throw for a wrong key or non-JSON plaintext. None of these are caught, so callers get a 500 with a Next.js error instead of a 4xx, and decryption stack traces end up in the logs. Add a `req.method !== "POST"` guard, use `safeParse`, and wrap the decrypt/parse in try/catch returning 400.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED holds the encryption key value instead of a boolean

`process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` evaluates to the value of `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (a secret) rather than `true`. The export is typed `string | undefined` and lives in a constants module that is imported broadly; any place that logs, serializes into props, or returns this constant would leak the AES key. Wrap it in `!!(...)` so only a boolean is ever exported.

No tests for the new OAuth sync helpers or webhook endpoint

`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens` and `/api/webhook/app-credential` are new shared primitives that touch every OAuth app's stored credentials, yet the PR adds no unit tests. The schema bug (computed `[z.string().toString()]` keys), the dummy `refresh_token` write, and the mismatched return shapes between call sites are exactly the kind of regressions a few table-driven tests on these two helpers (sharing enabled/disabled, response with and without refresh_token/expiry) plus a handler test for the webhook (bad secret, bad body, create vs update) would have caught.

Request to the credential sync endpoint is unauthenticated and its status is never checked

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret, signature, or auth header, so the self-hoster's token-vending endpoint cannot verify that the caller is Cal.com — anyone who can reach that URL can request a user's access token. The inbound direction (`/api/webhook/app-credential`) does require `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`; the outbound direction should be authenticated the same way. Additionally the response status is never checked (`response.ok`), so an error page/JSON from the endpoint flows into the token parsing and can be written to the credential.

Webex wires refreshOAuthTokens but still validates with the strict provider schema

Webex now fetches tokens through `refreshOAuthTokens` (so a sync endpoint may answer with just an access token and expiry) yet still validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires an exact `scope` literal, `token_type: "Bearer"`, `refresh_token` and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Any sync response will fail parsing and reject with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", so Webex credential sharing cannot work. Either use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` here (as zoom/office365 do) or don't route Webex through the sync helper.

Webhook secret compared with `!==` and header name not lowercased

The shared secret is compared with a plain string comparison, which is not constant-time; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Also, `req.headers` keys in Node are always lowercase, so if an operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` with any uppercase character the lookup silently returns `undefined` and every request is rejected with "Invalid webhook secret" — apply `.toLowerCase()` to the configured header name rather than relying on the comment in `.env.example`.

Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo" which is not the app's slug

`refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo`, but the Zoom app's slug in the app store / `Credential.appId` is `zoom` (see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts`, which creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`), and the inbound webhook resolves apps by `prisma.app.slug`. The self-hoster therefore receives a slug that does not correspond to any Cal.com app id, so token sync for Zoom is keyed on the wrong identifier.

`prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService

`await prisma.credential.update(...)` is added in `getClient()` but the file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a type-check failure and, at runtime, a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` on every Salesforce calendar operation (the constructor calls `getClient`), breaking the Salesforce app entirely.

findFirst + create is ambiguous for multi-credential apps and racy

Credentials are not unique per (userId, appId): a user can legitimately have several credentials for the same app (e.g. two Google Calendar accounts, and `larkcalendar`/`zoomvideo` callbacks explicitly deal with duplicates). `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key, and the payload has no way to identify which credential to update. Two concurrent webhook deliveries will also both miss the `findFirst` and create duplicate credentials. Consider requiring a credential identifier in the payload and/or performing the read-modify-write in a transaction.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist and duplicate filtering are case-sensitive, allowing bypass and duplicate attendees

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lower-cased when parsed from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, but the incoming `guest` string is compared as-is (`!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`). A caller can therefore bypass the blacklist entirely by sending `Blocked@Example.com` instead of `blocked@example.com`, and that address will be inserted as an attendee and emailed. The duplicate check `guest === attendee.email` has the same problem: an email that differs only in letter case from an existing attendee passes the filter and a second attendee row with the same mailbox is created. Normalize both sides with `toLowerCase()` (and trim) before comparing/inserting.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team permission check uses AND instead of OR, blocking team admins

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. Since `isTeamAdmin` already returns true for both ADMIN and OWNER roles, requiring both predicates means only team *owners* can pass this branch, and team admins are rejected with FORBIDDEN even though the variable name and the UI (`booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`) imply admins should be allowed. It should be `||` (or just `isTeamAdmin`). Additionally, for non-team bookings `booking.eventType?.teamId ?? 0` performs two pointless membership queries against team id 0 on every call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Raw input is passed to sendAddGuestsEmails instead of the filtered guest list

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the unfiltered request input. `sendAddGuestsEmails` treats every address in that list as a *new* guest and sends it the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a "your booking is confirmed" email). Any address that was in the request but filtered out as an already-existing attendee therefore receives a duplicate booking-confirmation email instead of the intended "guests added" notification. `uniqueGuests` (the list actually inserted) should be passed instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Input schema allows duplicate and unbounded guest lists

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no uniqueness refinement and no `.max()` limit. The uniqueness check only exists client-side in `AddGuestsDialog` (`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` with the Set refinement), so a direct tRPC call with `["a@b.com", "a@b.com"]` creates two identical attendee rows for the booking, and a call with thousands of addresses creates thousands of attendees and sends that many emails from the Cal instance (spam/abuse amplification). The server should de-duplicate and cap the list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type disableStandardEmails settings

Every other sender in this file gates host/attendee mail on `eventTypeDisableHostEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` (see `sendLocationChangeEmails` directly above). `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` argument and performs no such check, so event types configured with `metadata.disableStandardEmails.all.host/attendee` will still send organizer and attendee emails when guests are added, violating that setting. The handler should pass `booking.eventType?.metadata` and the sender should honour it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Booking `responses.guests` is not updated and no webhooks/workflows are triggered

Guests are inserted only into the `Attendee` table; the booking's `responses` JSON (which holds the `guests` booking field and is the source of truth used when the booking is rescheduled or re-rendered from booking fields) is left untouched, so added guests silently disappear on reschedule and are inconsistent with what the booking form shows. The handler also fires no webhook (`BOOKING_*`) and no workflow reminders for the new attendees, unlike other mutation handlers in this router, so integrations will not see the change.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` build the EventManager from the *logged-in* user, but this endpoint is explicitly reachable by attendees and team admins/owners (see the permission check above). When a non-organizer adds guests, `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is executed with credentials that do not include the calendar/video credential referenced by `booking.references`, so the external calendar event is not updated (or the update fails silently) and the newly added guests never appear on the organizer's calendar invite. The organizer (`booking.user`, already fetched with `credentials`) should be used to build the EventManager.

Clicking Add with no email rows does nothing and gives no feedback

When the user removes all email rows, `multiEmailValue.length === 0` and `handleAdd` returns silently: no toast, no inline error, no mutation. The button looks functional but is a no-op, which reads as a broken dialog. Either disable the Add button when the list is empty or surface the validation message.

Email failure is swallowed with a bare console.log

`catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` discards the actual error object, so an SMTP/template failure produces no actionable information in logs (the rest of the codebase uses `@calcom/lib/logger` with `safeStringify`). Log the error itself via the logger so these failures are diagnosable.

MultiEmail imports the @calcom/ui barrel from inside packages/ui, creating a cycle

`MultiEmail.tsx` lives in `packages/ui` but imports `Button, EmailField, Icon, Tooltip` from `@calcom/ui`, which is the package's own `index.tsx` — and that index now re-exports `./form/MultiEmailLazy` → `./MultiEmail`. This circular import can produce undefined components at module-init time depending on bundler evaluation order, and it also pulls the entire UI barrel into the dynamically imported chunk, defeating the purpose of the `MultiEmailLazy` code split documented in that file. Import the components from their relative paths (`../components/button`, `../components/form`, etc.) as the other files in `packages/ui/form` do.

No booking status check: guests can be added to cancelled/rejected/past bookings

The handler loads the booking by id only and never inspects `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. A caller can therefore add guests to a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking, which inserts attendees and sends `AttendeeScheduledEmail` with an ICS of `status: "CONFIRMED"` and `method: "REQUEST"` — i.e. new guests receive an invite for a meeting that no longer exists. The UI also exposes the action through `editBookingActions`, which is rendered for past bookings (`isBookingInPast && isConfirmed` branch in BookingListItem), so guests can be invited to meetings that already happened. Reject non-ACCEPTED/past bookings server-side.

No tests for the new addGuests handler

This PR adds a new authenticated mutation that writes attendees, mutates external calendars and sends mail, with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer / attendee / team admin-owner), blacklist filtering and de-duplication — but no unit or integration test is included. At minimum there should be tests covering: rejection for an unrelated user, acceptance for organizer/attendee/team admin, duplicate and blacklisted emails being filtered, and the emails being sent only for newly added guests.

Organizer email subject can be empty or crash on attendees[0]

The subject interpolates `this.calEvent.attendees[0].name`. New guests are created with `name: ""` in `addGuests.handler.ts`, and the attendee list passed into the event is built from `prisma.booking.update(... include: { attendees: true })` with no `orderBy`, so the first element is not guaranteed to be the original booker — the subject can render as "Guests Added:  with  at ...". If `attendees` were ever empty this line throws while building the mail payload. Use a defensive fallback (e.g. `attendees[0]?.name || organizer.name`) and order attendees deterministically.

Seated events: attendees added without BookingSeat records break seat accounting

For event types with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, each attendee of a booking represents a booked seat and has an associated `BookingSeat` row (used for per-seat cancel/reschedule links and for computing remaining seats). This handler inserts plain `Attendee` rows with no `bookingSeat`, so added guests consume seats without being counted/limited, cannot cancel or reschedule their seat, and the attendee list of a seated booking can exceed `seatsPerTimeSlot`. Seated bookings should either be rejected or handled explicitly.

Validation error state is never reset on success or dialog close

`setIsInvalidEmail(true)` is set in `handleAdd` but is only cleared by the Cancel button. On a successful mutation (`onSuccess`) and when the dialog is dismissed via the overlay/escape (`onOpenChange` → `setIsOpenDialog`), `isInvalidEmail` stays `true`, so the next time the dialog is opened the red "Emails must be unique and valid" message is displayed before the user has typed anything. Reset the flag in `onSuccess` and at the start of `handleAdd`.

findFirstOrThrow on `booking.userId || 0` yields an opaque 500 for userless bookings

`booking.userId` is nullable (e.g. dynamic group bookings or bookings whose user was deleted). In that case the query runs with `id: 0`, `findFirstOrThrow` raises a Prisma NotFound error that is not caught, and the client receives an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR instead of a meaningful message. Handle the null `userId` explicitly (the booking's `user` relation is already included in the first query and could be reused instead of this second round-trip).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount updated with a read-modify-write instead of an atomic increment

Both update calls set `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` based on the value read earlier in the request. If two cron invocations overlap (or the job is retried by the scheduler), both read the same value and both write the same result, so failures are undercounted and the reminder keeps being retried indefinitely. Use Prisma's atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteMany `retryCount > 1` branch is not scoped to SMS or to unscheduled reminders

The new OR branch in the `deleteMany` only filters on `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`. Unlike the first branch it does not constrain `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, so this SMS-only cron will permanently delete EMAIL and WHATSAPP WorkflowReminder rows as soon as any other code path starts incrementing `retryCount` for them (the column is shared by all methods). It also does not constrain `scheduled: false` / `referenceId: null`, so a reminder that eventually succeeded after failures (scheduled = true, referenceId = Twilio SID) can be deleted; once the row is gone the SID is lost and the queued Twilio message can no longer be cancelled if the booking is cancelled or rescheduled, meaning reminders get sent for dead bookings. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` and `scheduled: false` to this branch.

false_positives.candidate:
Falsy return from scheduleSMS (e.g. SMS sending locked) is treated as a permanent failure

`twilio.scheduleSMS` returns without a value in non-error cases such as the user/team being locked for SMS sending (`SMSLockState` / isLockedForSMSSending). The new `else` branch treats that undefined return as a failed attempt and increments `retryCount`, so after two cron runs the reminder row is deleted. Once the account is unlocked or reviewed, those reminders are gone and will never be sent. Locked/suppressed states should be distinguished from real scheduling failures and should not consume retries.

OR on unindexed retryCount defeats the existing WorkflowReminder index

WorkflowReminder has `@@index([method, scheduled, scheduledDate])`, which the previous delete predicate could use. The new top-level `OR` adds a branch on `retryCount`, which has no index; Postgres will typically fall back to a sequential scan of the whole WorkflowReminder table on every run of this cron. On a table of this size that is an expensive repeated scan. Consider running the retry-exhausted cleanup as a separate narrowly-filtered delete (e.g. `method: SMS, scheduled: false, retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) and/or adding an index covering it.

Reminders with no message or no recipient still loop forever

`retryCount` is only touched inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` or in the catch. A reminder whose `sendTo` resolves to null (e.g. SMS_ATTENDEE with no `booking.smsReminderNumber`) or whose template produces an empty body falls through silently: it stays `scheduled: false` with `retryCount: 0` and is re-fetched by every cron run until its scheduled date passes — the exact repeated-rescheduling problem this PR is meant to fix. These cases should also consume a retry (or be deleted/marked immediately).

Unguarded prisma.update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` added in the `catch` block is awaited without its own error handling. If it throws (e.g. Prisma P2025 because the row was deleted concurrently, or a connection error — likely exactly when the original error was a DB problem), the rejection propagates out of the `for` loop and out of the handler, so every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped and the endpoint returns a 500 instead of the previous behaviour of logging and continuing. Wrap it in its own try/catch.

retryCount is incremented for failures unrelated to SMS delivery

The `catch` wraps the whole per-reminder body, which includes `getCalEventResponses`, `prisma.profile.findFirst`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `bookingMetadataSchema.parse` and template rendering — not just `twilio.scheduleSMS`. Any transient failure there (DB hiccup, Twilio-wide outage, a bad metadata blob) now bumps `retryCount`, and after two cron runs the reminder is deleted for good even though its scheduled date may be days away. A short outage spanning two cron invocations would wipe out all pending SMS reminders instead of retrying them later. The counter should only be bumped for an actual send/schedule failure (or the deletion threshold should account for transient errors).

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fail-open fallback branch in getBaseConditions

In `getBaseConditions()` the branch `else if (filterConditions) { return filterConditions; }` returns the user-supplied filter conditions with no authorization predicate at all. It is unreachable today only because `getAuthorizationConditions()` always resolves to a non-null `Prisma.Sql` (worst case `1=0`), but the typing (`Promise<Prisma.Sql>`) makes the `authConditions &&` checks pointless dead code, and if the auth builder is ever changed to return `null`/empty the query silently becomes unauthenticated. Drop the dead branches or make the no-auth case return `NOTHING_CONDITION`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization/filter SQL fragments are returned without outer parentheses

`buildOrgAuthorizationCondition` (line 171-174), `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` (line 204-207) and `buildFilterConditions` (line 119-122) return top-level `A OR B` / `A OR B` expressions with no enclosing parentheses, and these fragments are exposed through the public `getAuthorizationConditions()` / `getFilterConditions()` methods. Any caller that composes them as `WHERE "createdAt" > ${x} AND ${authConditions}` gets `("createdAt" > x AND A) OR B` because `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, i.e. rows matching only `B` are returned regardless of the other predicates — an authorization bypass. Only `getBaseConditions()` currently wraps them. Wrap each composed fragment in parentheses at construction time (`Prisma.sql`((${acc}) OR (${condition}))``) so the returned SQL is safe in any context.

Caching tests deleted while the caching logic still exists

The whole `describe("Caching")` block (previously asserting that `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return the memoized value on the second call) was removed, but `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` are still implemented in the service (insightsBooking.ts lines 83-95). The `cachedFilterConditions` memoization relies on an `=== undefined` check to distinguish "not computed" from a cached `null`; that subtle logic is now completely untested. The caching tests should be ported to the new `Prisma.sql` expectations rather than deleted.

Constructor option type loosened, team scope without teamId now silently returns nothing

The constructor parameter type changed from the validated discriminated union `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the new flat `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions` (`scope: "user" | "org" | "team"`, `teamId?: number`). Passing `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without `teamId` now type-checks, fails the runtime zod parse, sets `this.options = null`, and the service silently produces `1=0`, i.e. insights show zero bookings instead of surfacing a programming error. Either keep the discriminated union in the public signature or throw / log when `safeParse` fails so misuse is detectable.

Only user-scope SQL is executed against the database; ANY() array bindings untested

The single test that actually runs SQL (`prisma.$queryRaw` with `getBaseConditions()`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose condition contains no array parameters. The newly introduced `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` / `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})` constructs for team and org scope are only compared as `Prisma.Sql` objects via `toEqual`, which validates the template strings but never that Postgres accepts the generated query or that Prisma binds a JS number array to a PG array correctly. A broken array binding, a wrong column name, or an invalid boolean comparison in those branches would pass CI. Add an integration test that executes `$queryRaw` with team- and org-scope base conditions and asserts the returned booking ids.

Public `findMany` removed with no callers updated

`findMany(findManyArgs)` was the only query-executing method on `InsightsBookingService` and has been replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which merely returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The PR touches only this file and its test, so any existing consumer that calls `insightsBookingService.findMany(...)` (e.g. insights tRPC routers) will fail to compile / break at runtime. Beyond the compile break, the enforcement point for authorization has moved out of the service into every caller: previously the auth conditions were guaranteed to be ANDed into the Prisma `where`; now a caller that forgets to interpolate `getBaseConditions()` into its raw query silently returns unfiltered booking data. Either keep a query helper on the service (e.g. `findAll`/`getRows` that builds the full SQL) or update and audit all call sites in this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unused updateMany with empty data on every cache refresh

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is executed after every `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` run (triggered by every Google webhook notification and by the watch cron) solely to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. It (a) relies on the implicit Prisma behaviour of emitting `SET updatedAt = now()` for an empty `data` object, which is fragile and non-obvious, (b) touches *all* selected calendars of the credential, including ones whose cache was not refreshed in this run, and (c) writes a value the PR itself states is not consumed anywhere (the UI reads `cacheUpdatedAt` from `CalendarCache`). It also silently no-ops for in-memory delegation credentials whose id is negative. Remove it or make the intent explicit with an actual `updatedAt: new Date()` payload scoped to the refreshed calendars.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dev script uses macOS-only sed syntax and masks failures

`sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD/macOS syntax; on Linux (GNU sed) the empty argument is parsed as the input filename and the command fails with "can't read : No such file or directory", leaving `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` un-updated. In addition `ENV_FILE="../.env"` only resolves correctly when the script is invoked from inside `scripts/`, and `cleanup()` always `exit 0`, so the "Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL" path returns a success exit status to the caller.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure throws plain Error → 500 instead of a tRPC error

When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC turns non-`TRPCError` throws into `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500) and reports them as unexpected server errors (noise in Sentry/logs), while the client only sees a generic failure. This should be `throw new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN" | "NOT_FOUND", message: ... })` so the status code and client handling are correct.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hard-coded to en-US formatting

`new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })` formats the cache timestamp with US date order and 12-hour clock for every user, ignoring the user's locale (available via `useLocale()`) and their 12/24h `timeFormat` preference. Non-US users will see a date like `7/15/25, 4:06 PM`, which is confusing/ambiguous. Pass the active locale (and ideally the user's time format) instead of a literal.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status ignores expiresAt, so expired cache is reported as present

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups all `CalendarCache` rows for the credential with no `expiresAt` filter. Rows stay in the table after they expire (lookups filter on `expiresAt >= now()`), so the UI will show a "Last updated" timestamp and offer "Delete cached data" for a credential whose cache is no longer usable, giving a misleading picture of cache health. Filter on `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` (or surface expiry separately).

Cache status/delete is unavailable for Delegation Credential connections

`hasCache` is derived from `cacheUpdatedAt`, which the handler resolves by matching `connectedCalendar.credentialId` against `CalendarCache.credentialId`. Delegation (domain-wide) connections surface in-memory credentials with negative ids, and their cache rows are looked up by `userId` (see `getCachedAvailability`'s `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` branch), so the map lookup never matches: for exactly the org users who most rely on calendar cache the dropdown is rendered as `null` (no cache status, no way to purge a bad cache). Either resolve cache status by userId for delegation credentials or document that the feature intentionally excludes them.

CalendarCacheRepository instantiated directly, bypassing the calendar-cache feature gate

The handler does `new CalendarCacheRepository()` instead of going through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the factory that returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the `calendar-cache` feature is disabled. As a result every `connectedCalendars` query now issues an extra `calendarCache.groupBy` query (this endpoint is called on the installed-apps and event-type calendar screens), and the UI will advertise "Cache Status"/"Delete cached data" for deployments or users where calendar cache is turned off. Use the existing factory so the feature flag is respected and the mock short-circuits the DB call.

Migration warning comment contradicts the actual SQL

The header says "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." while the statement below actually adds the column with `DEFAULT NOW()`. A reviewer or operator reading the migration will believe it is a destructive/blocking change on a non-empty table. Remove or correct the stale auto-generated warning.

No tests for the new cache status/delete paths

The PR adds a new mutation (`deleteCacheHandler`, including its ownership check), a new repository method (`CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), the credential→cache mapping in `connectedCalendarsHandler`, and a new UI component, with no unit or integration tests. At minimum the authorization branch of `deleteCacheHandler` (another user's credentialId must be rejected and must not delete rows) and the credentialId→updatedAt mapping should be covered, since a mapping bug would silently show one credential's cache state under another credential.

UserWithCalendars now requires updatedAt/googleChannelId that this module never reads

`allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars` in the exported `UserWithCalendars` type were widened to require `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId`, but nothing in `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb` (or the new cache-status code, which keys off `CalendarCache`) uses those fields.
