Every caller that builds this object from a narrower Prisma `select` (API v2 / platform-libraries call sites, onboarding handlers) now fails type-checking; the PR only updated one select (`UserRepository.findUnlockedUserForSession`). Either revert the type widening or update all the selects that feed this type.

deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query

The disconnect mutation invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`, but `deleteCacheMutation` only calls the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback (the `onChanged` prop, which is undefined in several call sites of `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper`). Since `cacheUpdatedAt` comes from that query and `connectedCalendars` is configured with `refetchOnWindowFocus: false`, after a successful deletion the dropdown keeps showing the old "Last updated" timestamp and the now-meaningless "Delete cached data" entry until a full page reload. Add `await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` to the mutation's onSuccess/onSettled.

dev:cron now runs an undeclared dependency via npx

`dev:cron` was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`. `tsx` is not in this package's (or the repo's) dependencies, so `npx` will download it from the registry at run time — the script fails offline/in restricted CI and pulls an unpinned package version (supply-chain risk). `ts-node` is still listed in devDependencies but unused by this script. Either add `tsx` as a devDependency and call it directly, or keep `ts-node`.

updateManyByCredentialId types data as SelectedCalendarUpdateInput but calls updateMany

`updateMany` accepts `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`, not `SelectedCalendarUpdateInput`. Because the parameter is typed with the latter, nested relation writes (e.g. `user: { connect: { id } }`, `eventType: { disconnect: true }`) type-check at the call site but are rejected by Prisma at runtime. Type the parameter as `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is now fire-and-forget and may never be committed

The previous code pushed `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` into `prismaPromises` and awaited them before returning. Now `deleteScheduledEmailReminder()` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder()` are async functions invoked inside `forEach` without `await` and their promises are never collected, so the handler can return its 200 response while the `prisma.workflowReminder.update({ data: { cancelled: true } })` (or the Twilio cancel + row delete) is still in flight. In a serverless deployment the function can be frozen/terminated right after the response, so the `cancelled` flag is never persisted and the reminder email is still delivered for the cancelled booking. Errors are also swallowed inside the helpers, so this fails silently.

The same pattern was introduced at `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx:488` (where `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)` was removed) and `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts:966`. These calls should be collected and awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path keeps the old failure mode and leaves the reminder row behind

When `immediateDelete` is true (used by the reschedule path in `handleNewBooking.ts:968`, the workflow-delete path and the deleted-step path in `workflows.tsx:214/521`) the function still performs a synchronous `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends { status: "cancel" }` and then returns.

Two problems:
1. This is exactly the call the PR description identifies as unreliable (SendGrid keeps cancelled batches in `scheduled_sends` and caps pending cancellations at 100). Any failure is swallowed by the surrounding `catch` that only `console.log`s, and because the row is neither marked `cancelled` nor deleted, the new CRON-based retry mechanism will never pick it up. The reminder email for the rescheduled booking is therefore still sent – the exact bug this PR claims to fix for rescheduled bookings.
2. Unlike the `!referenceId` branch (which deletes the row) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (which deletes the row), this branch leaves the `WorkflowReminder` row in the DB pointing at the old/cancelled booking until the cron's `deleteMany` eventually removes it when `scheduledDate` has passed.

For reschedules it would be safer to use the same deferred mechanism (set `cancelled: true`) instead of the one-shot immediate cancel.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New `cancelled` flag is nullable with no index backing the cron query

`cancelled Boolean?` (and the migration `ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN`) has no default, so every existing and newly created row stores NULL and all call sites must use `cancelled: true` rather than a boolean comparison (easy to get wrong later – `@default(false)` would be safer). More importantly, `WorkflowReminder` has no index on `cancelled`/`scheduledDate`, yet the new cron query `findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: ... } } })` – plus the existing `deleteMany` and unscheduled-reminder scan – runs every 15 minutes over a table that grows with every booking, resulting in repeated full table scans.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation query is not restricted to scheduled SendGrid email reminders

`remindersToCancel` selects every `WorkflowReminder` with `cancelled: true`, without filtering `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` or `referenceId: { not: null }`. The `cancelled` column is on the shared model, so any SMS row (or a row with a null `referenceId`) that ever gets `cancelled: true` would be sent to SendGrid as `batch_id: <twilio sid|null>`; the request fails and, per the single shared try/catch around the loop, aborts all remaining cancellations. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` and `referenceId: { not: null }` to the where clause.

Deferred cancellation can miss SendGrid's cancellation deadline for imminent reminders

Cancelling/rescheduling now never cancels the SendGrid send immediately; it only sets `cancelled: true` and relies on the `scheduleEmailReminders` cron (runs every 15 min, cancels reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour). SendGrid only honours a cancellation submitted sufficiently far ahead of the scheduled send (documented as at least 10 minutes). If a booking is cancelled, say, 12 minutes before the reminder's `sendAt`, the next cron tick can be up to 15 minutes later – i.e. after the send time – so the reminder email is still delivered for a cancelled/rescheduled booking. Consider cancelling immediately (and still marking `cancelled: true` so the cron can retry) when `scheduledDate` is close to now.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and skips all DB deletes

The `for` loop over `remindersToCancel` is wrapped in a single `try/catch`. If `client.request` throws for one reminder (invalid/expired batch id, rate limit, SendGrid 4xx/5xx), the loop is abandoned: every remaining reminder in this run is not cancelled, and – because `prisma.workflowReminder.delete()` returns a lazy `PrismaPromise` that is only executed when awaited at line 74 – none of the already-cancelled reminders are deleted either. A single permanently failing `referenceId` therefore blocks cancellation of every other reminder on every subsequent cron run, which reproduces the "reminders still sent" bug this PR fixes. Each iteration should have its own try/catch (and the delete should be awaited per reminder). The query also has no `take` limit, so a large backlog can exceed the function timeout.

Unused `Prisma` import and type-only identifiers moved into a value import

`Prisma` is added to the `@prisma/client` value import but is no longer used anywhere in the file (the only remaining use, `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>[]`, was deleted in this diff), which will fail `no-unused-vars` in CI. The same import also converts the previous `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise }` into a value import of type-only identifiers (also done in `handleNewBooking.ts:1-10` for `App`, `Credential`, `EventTypeCustomInput`, `Prisma`), which conflicts with the `import type` convention used throughout the repo/`consistent-type-imports`. Additionally the new member is added without a trailing comma (`Prisma\n} from "@prisma/client";`), so the prettier check will fail. The unrelated re-indentation of the large commented-out `testAction` block (lines ~901-1009) suggests this file was taken from an older branch; please rebase.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected app-import promises are created with no handler attached (unhandled rejection at startup)

Each value in `appStore` is a promise created at module load and stored for an indefinite amount of time before any consumer awaits it. If any one app module fails to evaluate (missing/incorrect peer dependency, module-scope code that throws, bad env configuration), the corresponding promise rejects with no `.catch()` attached, producing an unhandled promise rejection at process start — which terminates the Node process on Node >= 15. Previously a broken app module failed loudly and synchronously at import time with a clear stack trace; now it can either kill the server or silently surface later as a generic "Could not get connected calendars" error from `getConnectedCalendars`'s catch block. Promises for apps that are never used are never awaited at all, so their rejections are always unhandled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring-cancellation branch still uses forEach(async) so calendar deletions are never awaited

In the recurring/allRemainingBookings branch the code iterates credentials with `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); … apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. `forEach` does not await the async callbacks, so the handler continues immediately and `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at the end of the handler runs while `apiDeletes` is still empty for this path. Consequently, for recurring bookings the external calendar events are deleted fire-and-forget (and in a serverless runtime may never be deleted at all, since the response is returned before the awaited dynamic app import resolves), and any `deleteEvent` failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection instead of being surfaced. The adjacent legacy branch in this same PR was correctly converted to `for (const credential of calendarCredentials)`; the same conversion is needed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are started eagerly, so nothing is actually lazily loaded

`appStore` is now an object literal whose values are the *results* of calling `import("./app")` at module-evaluation time. Calling `import()` immediately starts loading the module, so every single app package (applecalendar, googlecalendar, stripepayment, …) is still pulled in as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is imported — the only thing that changed is that consumers now have to `await` the already in-flight promise. The PR's goal of async/lazy app loading is not achieved, while the extra `async`/`await` plumbing added across CalendarManager, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, bookings.tsx etc. buys nothing. To actually defer loading, the map must hold thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call sites must invoke them, e.g. `await appStore[key]()`.

Example comment points at a non-existent path

The template comment was changed from `// import * as example from "./_example";` to `// example: import("./example"),`. The example app lives in the `_example` directory, so anyone uncommenting/copying this line will get a module-not-found error. The commented path should be `./_example`.

forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves deletions unawaited

Same problem as in the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); … })` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that can no longer catch anything, because errors raised inside the async callbacks reject the (discarded) returned promises instead of propagating synchronously — they become unhandled promise rejections. Additionally the booking is marked cancelled and the reschedule email is sent before the awaited dynamic app import resolves, so the external calendar/video cancellation requests may never be issued. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))`.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in the `calendar` field, changing its public contract

`getCalendarCredentials` is exported and returns `{ integration, credential, calendar }`. Because `getCalendar` became async, `calendar` is now `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other caller that reads `.calendar` keeps a promise, which is always truthy, so guards like `if (!calendar)` silently pass and subsequent `calendar.listCalendars()` style calls fail at runtime. Additionally, these promises are created eagerly for every credential inside a non-async function, so if a caller only needs `integration`/`credential`, a rejected `getCalendar` promise is never handled. Either make the function async and await the calendars, or keep the field lazy (a thunk) and update all consumers.

requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events in an unawaited forEach(async) callback

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is not awaited, so the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule-request email, fire webhooks and return before the deletions are even initiated. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` requests were at least started before the handler continued; now the first thing the callback does is await a dynamic module import, meaning in a serverless/edge runtime the function can be frozen or torn down after the response and the stale calendar entries / video meetings will never be removed. Rejections are also unobserved (unhandled promise rejection). Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))` or a `for … of` loop.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is computed from the slot start, so the slot end is never validated

At lines 141-142 both `start` and `end` are computed as `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`; `end` should be derived from `slotEndTime` (slot start + eventLength). As written the `end > workingHour.endTime` comparison is equivalent to the `start` comparison, so a slot that begins inside working hours but runs past the end of the working-hours window is never rejected (e.g. a 60-minute event starting at 16:45 for a 09:00-17:00 schedule).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs instances compared with `===`, condition is always false

Line 114 compares two freshly created Dayjs objects with `===` (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references and is therefore always false. The intended case — a zero-length override marking the whole day unavailable — is never detected by this branch; use `.isSame()` (or compare `valueOf()`). As written the branch is dead code and gives a false impression of handling that case.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override day short-circuits the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, when a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls inside the override range, the function does `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` (line 133-135) and returns before ever evaluating `busy.every(...)`. This means that on any day that has a date override, existing bookings and external calendar busy times are completely ignored, so already-booked slots are offered again and can be double booked. The override check should only narrow availability (continue to the busy check) rather than grant it unconditionally.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make all slots unavailable

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` callback (lines 106-127) returns `true` when the slot is *outside* a given override range, and any truthy result makes the whole function return `false` (unavailable). Cal.com allows several time ranges for the same override date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00); a 09:30 slot is inside the first range but outside the second, so `find` matches the second range and the slot is dropped. The logic must consider the union of all override ranges for the day (slot is unavailable only if it is outside *every* range for that date).

No test for the fixed-host (round-robin) override fix, and only an eastward timezone is covered

The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events, but the only new assertion (lines 788-804) re-queries a single-user event type with Asia/Dhaka. There is no scenario with a round-robin event type having a fixed host with a date override plus an available round-robin host, so the new `checkIfIsAvailable` override/working-hours path is untested for the case it was written for. In addition, both tested timezones are east of the organizer's (+5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute shift), so the day-rollover case (an invitee timezone west of the organizer, e.g. America/Los_Angeles) — which is where the override conversion in packages/lib/slots.ts breaks — is not covered.

Override time conversion loses the day component, producing slots on the wrong day/time

The new override conversion (lines 216-224) computes minutes-since-midnight as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. When the timezone shift moves the override across midnight (e.g. organizer 10:00-11:00 in Asia/Kolkata viewed by an America/Los_Angeles invitee, offset = -750 min), the converted instant lands on the previous day but only hour/minute are kept, so the override is interpreted as 21:30-22:30 of the invitee's current day — roughly 24 hours away from the real time. For eastward shifts the same truncation can also yield `startTime > endTime`, producing no slots at all. The conversion needs to account for the day rollover (e.g. compute the diff in minutes from `startOfInviteeDay`) instead of truncating to hour/minute.

Override timezone is optional but used unguarded in `dayjs().tz()`

`override.timeZone` is declared optional in `TimeRange` (packages/types/schedule.d.ts) and is only populated by the new code in the slots tRPC router. Line 212 calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)`; with `undefined` dayjs silently falls back to the default/guessed timezone, so `organizerUtcOffset` becomes the server's offset and the computed `offset` shifts override slots by an arbitrary amount for any other caller of `getSlots` that passes `dateOverrides` without `timeZone`. Either make `timeZone` required for overrides reaching this code path or fall back explicitly to `organizerTimeZone`. Also note `override.start.toString()` relies on parsing a non-ISO `Date#toString()` value; passing the Date directly would be safer.

Override/slot day comparison mixes server-local time with UTC

Line 110 compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is a UTC dayjs object, but `dayjs(date.start)` is in the process-local timezone, so `.format()` renders the override date in whatever `TZ` the server runs with. On a server that is not UTC, overrides whose converted instant lies near midnight UTC will be compared against a different calendar day, so the override is silently not detected (falling through to the normal working-hours path) or matched on the wrong day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` so both sides are formatted in the same zone.

Working-hours check rejects a slot if ANY working-hours range does not contain it

The new block uses `workingHours.find(workingHour => ... slot outside this range ... return true)` and treats a truthy result as "slot is outside of working hours" (lines 138-151). `getUserAvailability`/`getWorkingHours` returns one entry per availability row, so a user with a split schedule (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 on the same days) has two entries for that weekday. A 10:00 slot is inside the first range but outside the second, so `find` returns the second entry and the slot is discarded. Because fixed hosts include the single user of personal event types, every user with more than one availability range per day will lose all of their slots. The condition needs to be "no range contains the slot" (`!workingHours.some(contains)`), not "some range does not contain it".

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, so the new identity check can be bypassed

`OAuthLoginView` sends `state=pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates `request.GET["state"] == pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the fully-qualified class names of the pipeline views, i.e. a value that is identical for every user and every session (the new test even hard-codes it as `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). It is therefore not a per-session nonce and provides no CSRF/session binding: an attacker who authorizes the GitHub OAuth app themselves can hand a victim a URL such as `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known_signature>`. The victim's pipeline will accept it, exchange the attacker's code, and bind `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker's login — which then matches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` and defeats exactly the installer-identity check this PR adds. Follow the existing pattern in `sentry.identity.oauth2` (`OAuth2LoginView` generates `secrets.token_hex()`, binds it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)`, and `OAuth2CallbackView` compares it with `constant_time_compare`).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError and return a 500

The new check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally. `sender` is only written by `build_integration` when the incoming state contains it (currently only the GitHub `installation` webhook path), so integrations created before that metadata existed, or by any flow where the webhook did not supply a sender, have no `sender` key. In that case the installation pipeline raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." dialog. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and fail closed) instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Authorize URL built by string interpolation without URL-encoding

`client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated raw into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` comes from `absolute_uri(...)` and can contain characters that must be percent-encoded in a query value (e.g. when the install URL carries a query string or when a custom `SENTRY_URL_PREFIX`/subdomain introduces reserved characters), which would silently corrupt the redirect GitHub uses. Build the query with `urlencode({...})` as `OAuth2LoginView` does.

Installer-identity check is skipped when the Integration row does not yet exist

The comparison between `github_authenticated_user` and the installing GitHub user only happens in the branch where an `Integration` row already exists (lines 493-505). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline immediately advances (line 482) and `build_integration` creates the integration with no identity validation at all. Since that row is created asynchronously by the GitHub `installation` webhook, an attacker who completes the Sentry pipeline before the webhook is processed (or on an instance where the webhook is not delivered) still gets the previous, unvalidated behaviour. Consider validating the authenticated user against the installation data returned by `get_installation_info()` (e.g. the account/sender) in that path as well, so the protection does not depend on a webhook race.

Unhandled exception from `get_user_info` / `safe_urlopen` yields a 500 instead of the error dialog

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` performs an HTTP call and raises on non-2xx responses (`raise_for_status`), and `safe_urlopen` on line 423 can raise on network/timeout errors. Neither is wrapped in a try/except, so a transient GitHub failure or a revoked/invalid token during installation surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the setup popup rather than the `github-integration-failed.html` dialog that the rest of this view carefully returns. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure (ideally with logging so these failures are diagnosable).

`_(error_short)` cannot be extracted for translation

`error()` calls `_(error_short)` on a runtime variable. The literal strings passed by callers ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization.") are no longer wrapped in `_()` at their definition sites, so `makemessages` will not extract them and they will never be translated (the long messages are correctly marked, the short ones are not). Mark the short strings with `gettext_lazy` at the call sites and drop the runtime `_()`.

`test_installation_not_found` no longer tests installation-not-found

The test still stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` but now passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used everywhere else in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore fails in `OAuthLoginView` on the state check and the assertion only verifies the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The previously covered behaviour — `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` for a 404 from GitHub — is now untested, and nothing covers the missing-`access_token` or user-mismatch-in-OAuthLoginView branches separately. Use the correct state so the test reaches `GitHubInstallation`/`build_integration`, and add a distinct test for the state-mismatch path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` makes the default value a class-level constant computed when the module is first imported, not when an `AssignmentSource` is constructed. Every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` (which never passes `queued`) will therefore carry the process start/import timestamp, which can be hours or days stale. Any present or future logic that reasons about how long ago the assignment was queued (e.g. expiring the cycle-breaking context) will be silently wrong, and the field's value is misleading in logs/payloads. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`to_dict`/`from_dict` do not survive a Celery JSON round-trip with a typed `queued`

`to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, so `queued` is a raw `datetime` that is handed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={... "assignment_source_dict": ...})`. Celery/kombu's JSON serializer will encode it as an ISO-8601 string (and a stricter serializer would reject it outright), and `from_dict` simply does `cls(**input_dict)` with no coercion, so the reconstructed object's `queued` is a `str` even though it is annotated `datetime`. Anything that later compares or arithmetics on `queued` will raise `TypeError` at runtime. Serialize `queued` explicitly (e.g. `isoformat()`) and parse it back in `from_dict`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
Cycle-breaking is only tested for assign, not deassign, and never through the task boundary

There is a new test for `assign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` not triggering outbound sync, but no equivalent test for `deassign(..., assignment_source=...)`, even though `sync_group_assignee_inbound` now passes a source on the unassign path. Also, all tests run under `self.tasks()` (eager execution), so `assignment_source_dict` is handed to the task as a live `dict` with a `datetime`; the serialize/deserialize path used in production (and therefore `AssignmentSource.from_dict` receiving a string `queued`) is never exercised. A regression in that path would silently restore the sync loop without failing any test.

Malformed assignment source is silently dropped, re-enabling sync cycles

`from_dict` swallows `ValueError`/`TypeError` and returns `None`. In `sync_assignee_outbound` the returned `None` is passed to `should_sync("outbound_assignee", None)`, which means the cycle-prevention check is skipped entirely and the change is propagated back to the originating integration — exactly the loop this PR is meant to break. Since this failure mode is invisible (no log, no metric), a payload-shape change (e.g. the `queued` serialization issue above, or an added/renamed field during a deploy) would silently reintroduce the sync loop. Log/capture the parse failure instead of returning `None` silently.

New positional second argument to `should_sync` can break duck-typed installations

The task only checks `hasattr(installation, "should_sync")` and now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` with two positional arguments. Any installation class that defines `should_sync(self, attribute)` with the old single-argument signature (only the two definitions in `mixins/issues.py` were updated here) will now raise `TypeError`, which the `@retry` decorator will retry 5 times before giving up — silently breaking outbound assignee sync for that provider. Additionally the parameter is named `sync_source` in `should_sync` but `assignment_source` everywhere else, so keyword calls will not be interchangeable; align the names and verify no other `should_sync` overrides exist.

No test covers the dict round-trip or the per-instance `queued` default

The new tests only assert that `to_dict()["queued"]` is not `None` and that `from_dict` works for a dict without `queued`. They never (a) assert that `queued` differs between two instances created at different times, which would have caught the import-time default evaluation bug, nor (b) round-trip `to_dict()` through JSON serialization and back into `from_dict`, which is exactly how the value travels in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async`. Both the real failure modes of this dataclass are therefore untested.

`sync_status_outbound` gains an `assignment_source` parameter that is never passed or implemented

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature now declares `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`, but no caller passes it (the status-sync task still calls `sync_status_outbound(external_issue, is_resolved, project_id)`), no concrete integration implementation was updated, and `should_sync("outbound_status")` is still invoked without a source. The parameter is dead API surface that suggests status sync cycles are now broken when they are not; subclasses that only accept `**kwargs` would silently swallow the argument if someone starts passing it. Either wire the status path through (task kwarg + `should_sync` call + implementations) or drop the parameter from this signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and will raise TypeError when instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed to subclass `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass` as a body. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`), none of which are implemented here, so the class remains abstract. `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates the registered handler via `group_type.detector_handler(self)`; for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` this now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler ...` instead of returning a handler (previously it returned a no-op handler whose `evaluate` returned an empty list). Any code path that resolves the handler for a metric alert detector will crash rather than no-op. Either implement the abstract methods (even as stubs raising NotImplementedError only when actually called) or keep it on the non-abstract base until the real implementation lands.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Docstring still says evaluate returns a list

`StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still reads "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`. There will be one result for each group key result in the packet". This misdescribes the return contract for implementers/callers; update it to describe the dict keyed by group key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multi-group test builds expected occurrence with the wrong value

`test_state_results_multi_group` sends `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}` but constructs the expected occurrence for `group_2` with `value=6` (`build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`). The assertion only passes because the mock builder ignores the `value` argument entirely, so the test does not verify that `evaluate_group_key_value` passes the correct group value into `build_occurrence_and_event_data` — a regression in that argument would go undetected. Either pass 10 and make the mock occurrence depend on `value` (e.g. in `evidence_data`), or assert on the hook arguments directly.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale TODO comment about stateful detector

The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` sits directly above a class that now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler`, so the TODO is already satisfied and is misleading. It should be removed or replaced with the remaining work (implementing the abstract hooks).

get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty

In `get_state_data`, `counter_updates` is initialized to `{}` and only populated inside `if self.counter_names:`. The result loop then unconditionally does `counter_updates=counter_updates[gk]`, which raises `KeyError` for every group key when a subclass legitimately declares `counter_names = []`. With the new `StatefulDetectorHandler` hook being the intended base for real detectors (e.g. metric alerts, which may not need counters), this will blow up during evaluation. Use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` or build a default dict of `{name: None}` per group key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`get_monitor_environment_context` returns the raw config, discarding the humanized `schedule_type`

The function copies `monitor.config` into `config` and replaces the numeric `schedule_type` with its display value, but the returned dict sets `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config` — the original object, not `config`. The computed copy is dead code, so the monitor context attached to the issue occurrence event contains the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of the human readable one (e.g. `0` rather than `crontab`). Since this code is being moved into a new module anyway, it is a good time to return `config` instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring of `get_failure_reason` is misspelled and documents output the function cannot produce

The docstring reads "Builds a humam readible string" (should be "human readable") and lists example outputs that do not match the implementation: "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected" (the code emits "2 missed, 1 timeout and 1 error check-ins detected") and "A failed check-in was detected", which is never returned by any branch. Since the code is being moved into a new module, the docstring should be corrected so it doesn't mislead future readers about the generated user-facing text.

Public names removed from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` with no importers updated

This PR deletes the module-level names `mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context` and the `SimpleCheckIn` TypedDict from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and re-homes them (under new names in some cases) in `sentry/monitors/logic/incidents.py`, `sentry/monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py` and `sentry/monitors/types.py`. No other file in the PR is updated. Any production module or test that imports these symbols from `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed`, or that monkeypatches them by path (e.g. `mock.patch("sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence")`), will now raise ImportError/AttributeError, or worse, silently patch nothing and let real Kafka occurrences be produced in tests. The reorganization should be accompanied by updates to all call sites/patch targets (grep for the old names) before merging.

`get_failure_reason` produces a malformed string when no statuses are recognized

`status_counts` only counts statuses present in `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP` (error/missed/timeout). If `failed_checkins` is empty or contains only other statuses (e.g. `IN_PROGRESS`/`OK`), the counter is empty, the `sum(...) == 1` branch is skipped, `get_text_list([])` returns an empty string and the function returns the nonsensical " check-ins detected", which is then shown to users as the issue's "Failure reason" evidence. A fallback such as the generic "A failed check-in was detected" message mentioned in the docstring should be returned for the empty case.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard groups

The produce timer and segment size metrics are tagged `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195) while the wait_produce timer is tagged `{"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199) — two different tag keys for the same dimension, which will silently split dashboards/queries. Worse, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,3,6"`), whose value depends on the Kafka partition assignment of each consumer instance and changes on every rebalance. `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment, so this adds a per-assignment, unbounded-cardinality tag to a very high-volume metric. Use a single stable tag key and either omit the shard tag or emit one metric per concrete shard.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62, whose comment claims to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore returns immediately and provides no synchronisation at all. The test still races: if the flusher thread has not observed the new `current_drift` before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails with a ValueError. Either use a real sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before patching) or poll on `messages` with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for spawn processes, so unhealthy flushers are never killed

`self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates processes of type `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` never fires, and the previous unconditional `self.process.kill()` behaviour is lost. Consequence: when a flusher is declared unhealthy (hang or non-responsive), the old OS process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards()` immediately starts a second process for the *same* shards. Two processes then call `flush_segments()`/`done_flush_segments()` on the same Redis shards, which can produce duplicated segments to `buffered-segments` and leaks a process on every restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per shard group). The same wrong check is used in `join()` (line 346), so `terminate()` is also never called on shutdown. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62, whose comment claims to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore returns immediately and provides no synchronisation at all. The test still races: if the flusher thread has not observed the new `current_drift` before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails with a ValueError. Either use a real sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before patching) or poll on `messages` with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons remaining processes once the deadline expires

In `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time` only to `break` out of the whole loop when the deadline has passed. Processes later in the iteration order are then neither waited on nor terminated, so on a timed-out shutdown an arbitrary subset of flusher processes is left running (they are daemons, so they die only when the parent exits). The computed `remaining_time` is otherwise unused — the inner wait loop re-checks `deadline` instead, so the first process can consume the entire timeout. Terminate every process regardless of the deadline.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused and silently no-ops for unknown shards

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` has no callers anywhere after the refactor (health checking now goes through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). It is also subtly unsafe: if the shard is not found in `process_to_shards_map` it silently does nothing. Leaving it in invites a future caller to use the wrong restart path; delete it.

Docstring claims one process per shard and omits the new max_processes parameter

The class docstring now says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the `process-spans` consumer defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, i.e. a single process handling all shards. The docstring's parameter list documents `topic` (which is not a parameter) and `produce_to_pipe`, but not the new `max_processes` argument or its `None` default (one process per shard). This will mislead operators tuning the flusher.

New flusher test asserts a tautology and never exercises the multiprocess path

`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` is trivially satisfied by the construction loop and would still pass if a shard were assigned twice while another was dropped. The meaningful invariant — that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals the assigned shards exactly once each — is not checked. In addition, because `produce_to_pipe` is passed, `SpanFlusher` takes the `threading.Thread` branch, so the test does not cover the actual `SpawnProcess` path this PR introduces (process creation, pickling of the per-shard `SpansBuffer`, restart/kill logic), and the factory is never shut down (`fac.shutdown()` is not called).

No validation of flusher_processes; negative value raises KeyError, 0 silently means one process per shard

`--flusher-processes` is parsed as a plain int with no range validation and is used as `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` / `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`. With `--flusher-processes 0`, `0 or N` evaluates to `N`, so the operator silently gets one process per assigned shard instead of the obvious interpretation. With a negative value, `range(self.num_processes)` is empty while `i % self.num_processes` still evaluates to 0, so the shard assignment loop raises `KeyError: 0` and the consumer crashes at startup with an opaque error. Validate the option (>= 1) in the click option or in `__init__`.

Parent-side SpansBuffer per process is replaced on restart without closing the old one

`_create_process_for_shards()` constructs a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process on every (re)start and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent uses these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so they hold live Redis connections; the overwritten buffer is never closed, so each flusher restart leaks the old buffer's Redis client(s) in the main consumer process until GC. Note also that the `buffer` argument passed to `SpanFlusher` is now used only for `assigned_shards` — the extra parent-side buffers duplicate the Redis clients already held by the span-writing buffer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring and only passes because of commit timing

The test is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages" but asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing was committed. It passes only because the test breaks out of its wait loop after ~0.3s while the commit thread's first tick is at 1.0s; the implementation marks offsets complete in the worker's `finally` even on failure, so offset 102 *would* be committed a moment later. The test therefore verifies nothing about error handling and will flip to failing on any timing change. It should wait for the commit tick and assert the intended behaviour explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued items are discarded despite immediate=False

`shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` with the intent of letting workers drain remaining items. But `OrderedQueueWorker.run` re-checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker processes at most one more item and exits; everything still queued is dropped. This makes the "gracefully shutdown" docstring wrong and means a shutdown under load discards all buffered work (it will be reprocessed, since those offsets stay outstanding, but the drain the code appears to implement never happens). Either drain first and set the flag afterwards, or use `shutdown(immediate=True)` and don't pretend to drain.

Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs and a fixed 5-second wall-clock loop

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo internals that can change without notice), busy-loops for a hard-coded 5 seconds, and then asserts exact committed offsets. This makes the test slow and timing-dependent (a slow CI run that produces/consumes late will fail), and the `verify_consumer` is left unclosed if any assertion fails. Prefer the public `StreamProcessor.run()`/shutdown path or a condition-based wait with a generous timeout.

OffsetTracker never cleans up revoked partitions and keeps stale last_committed values

`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed` and `partition_locks` grow per partition and are never pruned when partitions are revoked. Because the tracker lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, a partition that is revoked and later reassigned keeps its old `last_committed` value; if the consumer re-reads from a lower offset (normal after a rebalance), `get_committable_offsets` will refuse to commit anything for that partition until the stream passes the stale high-water mark, and the offsets below it are reprocessed without ever being committed. Add a way to drop per-partition state on revocation.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which is arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback mutates the `KafkaConsumer`'s staged-offset state and may call `commit_offsets()` while the main processor thread is concurrently polling and running rebalance callbacks (which also stage/commit offsets). This state is not lock-protected, and staging offsets for a partition that was just revoked raises `ConsumerError("cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions")`. That error is swallowed by the loop's broad `except Exception`, so commits can silently stop working after a rebalance while processing continues. Commits should be driven from `poll()`/the main thread instead of a separate thread.

Per-item queue_depth gauge is emitted by all workers with identical tags, making the metric meaningless

Every worker emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only `{"identifier": ...}` as tags, once per processed item. With N workers the samples overwrite each other (last writer wins) so the gauge reflects a random worker's queue rather than anything interpretable, while paying statsd overhead on every message. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or emit aggregate depth from `poll()` only (which already publishes `queue_pool.total_queued`).

Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then silently drops all messages

`self.queue_pool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (line 133) and handed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo destroys and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/assignment, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every work queue. After the first rebalance a new strategy is created around the now-dead pool: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown` and every worker thread has exited. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` wraps everything in `except Exception` and then marks the offset as added+completed, those messages are never processed but their offsets are committed — i.e. total, silent data loss for the rest of the process lifetime. The pool must be owned by the strategy (recreated per assignment) or `shutdown()` must not be called from the strategy's close path.

Work queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and unbounded memory growth

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if one group's processing is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), arroyo will keep polling Kafka and the corresponding queue will grow without limit until the process OOMs. The problem is amplified because `WorkItem` also retains the whole `Message[KafkaPayload]` (line 31) even though only `partition`/`offset` are used, so each queued item holds the full Kafka payload alive. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or otherwise block) when full.

Worker marks offsets complete even when result processing raised, so failed messages are committed

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so a message whose `result_processor` raised an unexpected exception is logged and then its offset is committed. This silently converts processing failures into permanent message loss and diverges from the serial/batched modes, where an unhandled exception propagates to arroyo and can be DLQ'd or crash the consumer rather than being committed away. If skip-on-error is intended it should be explicit (and metered), not a side effect of `finally`.

close()/join() stop the commit thread before draining work, so completed work is never committed

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()` (which drains/stops workers). Any item processed after the last 1-second commit tick therefore has its offset marked complete but never committed, so it is reprocessed after restart. For uptime results this means duplicate processing of check results (duplicate status transitions/incidents) on every deploy. `join(timeout)` (line 344) also ignores its `timeout` argument and delegates to `close()`, which can block for up to ~5s per worker plus 5s for the commit thread, violating arroyo's shutdown deadline. A final `get_committable_offsets()` + `commit_function(..., force=True)` should run after the queues are drained.

submit() swallows every exception and marks the offset as completed, committing unprocessed messages

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception raised by the decoder, the grouping function, or `queue.put()` is caught by the blanket `except Exception`, logged, and then the offset is added and immediately completed so the commit loop will commit it. That means transient or structural failures (closed queue, grouping bug, OOM-adjacent errors, a `FilteredPayload` hitting the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`) result in the message being permanently skipped and its offset committed, with no DLQ and no retry. Only genuinely undecodable payloads should be fast-forwarded; everything else should propagate so arroyo can DLQ or crash the consumer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually prove the short-circuit

The new sub-test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` while the comment claims "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". A value of `false` means `checkPermission` would deny anyway, and the fallback path uses the default `fakeStore` (no permissions), which also denies. The assertion `assert.False(t, resp.Allowed)` therefore passes whether or not the new `permDenialCache` short-circuit at the top of `Check` works. To actually cover the new behaviour the scope map must grant access (`"dashboards:uid:dash1": true`) so that the test fails if the denial cache is ignored. Additionally there is no test asserting that `permDenialCache` is written after a DB-confirmed denial (service.go:153-155), so that half of the new logic is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key built from unescaped '_'-joined fields can collide

`userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `action`, `name` and `parent` with `_` separators and no escaping, so distinct requests can produce the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="" and name="a", parent="b_" both yield `...<action>_a_b_`. Dashboard/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores and are user-chosen, so a crafted (or merely unlucky) pair of UIDs makes a cached denial for one resource deny access to an unrelated resource for up to the 30s TTL (availability/incorrect-deny, not escalation, since only denials are stored). The key also omits group/resource, relying on `action` to encode them. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions or include explicit length/field delimiters.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID instead of the resolved user UID

`permDenialKey` uses `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw value parsed from the subject, while `permCache` keys use the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID` (see `getCachedIdentityPermissions`/`getUserPermissions`). Because `GetUserIdentifiers` treats a numeric subject as a user ID, the same identity addressed as `user:1` and as `user:<uid>` gets two independent denial entries (wasted lookups/queries), and a user whose UID is literally a decimal number shares denial entries with the user whose internal ID equals that number, which can deny the wrong identity for the TTL. Resolve the identifiers first and build the denial key from `userIdentifiers.UID` for consistency.

Every non-allowed Check now hits the database; denial cache is per (name, folder) and unbounded

The cache lookups were removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (a real `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` query) whenever the cached scope map does not already allow the request. The only protection against repeated queries is `permDenialCache`, whose key includes the resource name and parent folder (cache.go:30) and whose TTL is only 30s. Consequently a caller that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (object-by-object checks, or a client enumerating names) produces one uncached DB permission query per unique (action, name, folder) tuple, and fills the shared local cache with one entry per tuple (the authlib local cache has no size bound), so both DB load and memory are driven by caller-controlled input. This amplification is worse in-proc because the client-side cache was also disabled (rbac.go:103). Consider keeping a bounded/short-lived "permissions were just fetched" marker per (user, action) so the full re-query happens at most once per short interval rather than once per resource.

Stale folder tree still causes denials, and those denials are now cached

`Check` now re-queries permissions from the DB when the cached scope map does not allow the request, but `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still returns the cached folder tree (30s TTL) and is never refreshed when the requested parent folder is absent from it. So for a resource whose access is granted only through inheritance from an ancestor (e.g. a dashboard created in a brand-new subfolder of a folder the user has permissions on), the tree does not yet contain the new folder, the check denies, and the denial is then stored in `permDenialCache` (line 154), extending the window during which the user cannot see the newly created object. The stated goal of the PR (immediate access to newly created folders/dashboards) is therefore only met for directly-granted scopes. Consider re-fetching the folder tree (or at least not caching the denial) when `req.ParentFolder` is not present in the cached tree.

permissionCacheUsage metric is mislabelled on the new Check paths

In `Check`, a denial-cache hit increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="true"}` (line 118) even though the permission cache was not consulted at all, conflating two different caches in one metric. Conversely, when the permission cache *is* hit but the result is "not allowed", execution continues and line 137 increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="false"}`, reporting a cache miss for a request that was served from the cache. Cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts built on this metric will be wrong after this change; the denial cache should get its own metric and the hit label should reflect whether `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in the filtered list

In the `case 'grafana'` branch the newly used `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` is rendered without the `key={key}` prop that the previous `<GrafanaRuleLoader>` had (the other branches still pass `key`). The surrounding `rules.map(...)` produces a list, so React will log the "Each child in a list should have a unique key" warning and fall back to index-based reconciliation. Because this list is appended to incrementally during infinite scrolling, index-based reconciliation can reuse the wrong component instances (stale internal state such as open menus/drawers) for the wrong rule.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Silence notifications" menu item is a no-op when only a Prometheus rule is available

`canSilence` in AlertRuleMenu is now satisfied by the Prometheus-rule abilities (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`), so the "Silence notifications" item is rendered in the new list view. However the drawer is still rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true (line 104), and `rule` (the ruler rule) is `undefined` for list-view items that only pass `promRule`. Clicking the menu item therefore sets `showSilenceDrawer` but nothing ever opens — a dead menu entry. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts the item exists but never clicks it, so this is not caught. The drawer needs a path that works from the Prometheus rule (e.g. lazily fetch the ruler rule when opening) or the item must be hidden when no ruler rule is available.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items can never render in the ruler-free list view

The menu now computes Delete/Pause abilities from the Prometheus rule (`grafanaDeleteAbility`, `grafanaPauseAbility`), but the rendering of those items is still gated on the ruler rule being present: `{canDelete && rulerRule && ...}` (line 165) and `{canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...}` (line 123). Since the new rule list (GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons with only `promRule`) no longer loads ruler rules, `rulerRule` is always `undefined` there, so Delete and Pause disappear from the alert rule list menu even for users with permission. This is a user-visible regression: rules can no longer be deleted or paused from the list view. Either the gates must be relaxed to work from `promRule` (deriving the identifier/pause mutation from the Prometheus rule) or the actions must be hidden consistently with the computed abilities.

Federated rule group check dropped from useAllAlertRuleAbilities

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and treated federated groups as immutable, hiding Update/Delete/Pause. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. As a result every consumer of `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (rules table, rule details, rule viewer) will now offer Edit/Delete for Mimir/Cortex federated rule groups (groups with `source_tenants`). Editing such a group through the UI, which has no notion of `source_tenants`, can silently drop the federation configuration on save. The federated check should be preserved (the group/`source_tenants` information is available on the CombinedRule) before merging.

Grafana-managed recording rules lose Pause and Export abilities in the Prometheus ability hook

`useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` uses `isAlertingRule = prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` as the "is Grafana managed" flag for `Pause`, `ModifyExport`, `Restore` and `DeletePermanently`. The ruler-based equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)`, which is true for both Grafana alerting *and* Grafana recording rules. Grafana-managed recording rules support pausing and export, so after this change the list view will report Pause/ModifyExport as unsupported for them and the corresponding actions disappear. The flag should be `prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` for these abilities, with `alertingRule` reserved for alerting-only concerns such as Silence.

Provisioned-rule protection in the new list depends on an untested optional `provenance` field

`provenance` is added as an optional field on `GrafanaPromRuleDTOBase` and is the only signal used by `isProvisionedPromRule` (utils/rules.ts) and `GrafanaRuleListItem`'s `isProvisioned` flag now that the ruler response is no longer fetched in the list view. If the Grafana Prometheus rules endpoint does not populate `provenance` (it is optional, so a missing value is silently falsy), provisioned/file-provisioned rules will be rendered as editable and expose Edit/Delete actions that the API will later reject. There is no test in this PR covering a provisioned Grafana rule in the list view; one should be added (and the API response confirmed to include `provenance`).

Rule view link no longer carries the `returnTo` parameter

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader.GrafanaRuleListItem` built the href as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`. The new component drops the `returnTo` query parameter entirely. Consequently navigating from the rule list into a rule detail page loses the "return to previous" context, so the back/return affordance on the rule view will not bring the user back to the filtered list they came from. If this is intentional it should be stated; otherwise `createReturnTo()` should be re-added.

Test codifies the missing Delete/Pause actions and never exercises Silence

The new test asserts `menuItems.length).toBe(4)` (silence, copy link, duplicate, export) while the user has been granted `AlertingRuleDelete`/`AlertingRuleUpdate` both globally and on the folder. Delete and Pause are missing purely because AlertRuleMenu still requires a ruler rule to render them, so this assertion locks in the regression instead of detecting it. In addition, the `delete` selector added to `ui.menuItems` is never used, and the silence item is only asserted to exist — it is never clicked, which is why the non-functional silence drawer (it requires a ruler rule) goes unnoticed. The test should assert the full expected action set, including a click-through for Silence/Delete.

logWarning is called from the render body on every render

`getEditableIdentifier` is invoked directly during render and calls `logWarning('Unable to construct an editable rule identifier')` when neither a ruler rule nor a Grafana Prometheus rule is available (e.g. a data-source Prometheus rule with no ruler counterpart). Because this is a side effect inside render, the warning is emitted on every re-render (and twice per render under StrictMode) for each affected row, which can flood the analytics/log backend on a list page with many such rules. The logging should be moved into an effect or deduplicated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
New interpolation test mocks replace() so it cannot show $__auto is actually resolved up-front

The test supplies a `replace` implementation that unconditionally rewrites `$__auto` and `$step` regardless of the `scopedVars` it is given. Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__interval_ms`/`__range*` from `scopedVars` because those are interpolated on the backend, so in production `$__auto` will still be present in the expression after this new front-end interpolation step and will be resolved per sub-request range on the backend — i.e. the behaviour the linked issue complains about. With the current mock the assertion on `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])` passes no matter what `applyTemplateVariables` does with `$__auto`, giving false confidence that the issue is fixed. The test should drive interpolation through realistic `scopedVars` (including `__auto`) and a `replace` that honours them.

Shard path interpolates, then delegates to runSplitQuery which interpolates again

`runShardSplitQuery` interpolates all targets here, builds a sub-request whose expressions already contain the shard matcher (`__stream_shard__=~"..."` / `| drop __stream_shard__`), and then passes it to `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which — after this PR — interpolates every target once more, and `datasource.runQuery` triggers a third pass inside `DataSourceWithBackend.query`. The repeated `applyTemplateVariables` calls re-run `addAdHocFilters` on the shard-rewritten expression, so ad-hoc filters can be added two or three times (duplicated matchers, and for non-indexed labels filter stages appended after the injected `drop` stage). The updated test at shardQuerySplitting.test.ts:112 (`applyTemplateVariables` expected to be called 5 times for one target) is direct evidence of this redundancy; it only passes because the mock returns the same object unchanged after the first call.

Targets are now interpolated twice (runSplitQuery + DataSourceWithBackend.query)

`runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but each sub-request is later executed with `datasource.runQuery(subRequest)`, which goes through `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` and applies `applyTemplateVariables(q, request.scopedVars, request.filters)` again to the same (already interpolated) target. The second pass is not a no-op: Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` calls `addAdHocFilters(target.expr, adhocFilters)`, so ad-hoc filters are injected into the expression a second time (duplicated label matchers / duplicated `| key="value"` stages), and `templateSrv.replace` runs again over the already-substituted expression, so a variable value that itself contains a `$`-prefixed token gets expanded a second time. It also costs an extra LogQL parse/rewrite per sub-request. Either the pre-interpolation needs a way to mark targets as already interpolated, or the interpolation must stay in a single place.

Test asserts a magic call count that encodes redundant interpolation, and the mutating mock hides repeat interpolation

`expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` locks in the fact that one target is interpolated once in `runShardSplitQuery` plus once per sub-request inside `runSplitQuery`. Because the mock mutates and returns the same query object (`query.expr = query.expr.replace('$SELECTOR', ...)`), the extra calls are no-ops and the test cannot detect side effects of repeated interpolation such as duplicated ad-hoc filters. Any future change to the number of shard groups will also break this assertion for reasons unrelated to interpolation. A test asserting that ad-hoc filters/variables are applied exactly once to the final expression would be more meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID may disappear from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line

The explicit `traceID` field (previously obtained with `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)`, i.e. including non-sampled traces) was removed from `logParams` and is now expected to come from the contextual logger via `FromContext`. The contextual attributes added by `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` do not include a trace ID, so the field is only present if a globally registered contextual log provider injects it — and if that provider requires a sampled span, non-sampled requests will no longer have `traceID` in the `grafana-data-egress` log line. This silently breaks log queries/dashboards that correlate plugin egress logs with traces. Either keep adding `traceID` explicitly or confirm the provider semantics match the previous `requireSampled=false` behaviour.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a throwaway logger, so log calls become unobservable in tests

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` — a brand new, unrelated instance — instead of the receiver (`f`). Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, every log line recorded by the middleware is written into a discarded logger.
