true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Javadoc for getShortcut() says '3-letters' but the encoder requires exactly 2 characters

The Javadoc states the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters shortcut of specific grants", while all in-tree implementations return 2 characters and `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId()` hard-requires the encoded prefix to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type). A custom grant type that follows the Javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut would produce access-token ids that the very same provider cannot decode (`IllegalArgumentException: ... Expected length of 6`). The contract must state exactly 2 characters (and ideally be enforced).

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes because of an NPE, not the expected validation

The test constructs the factory without calling `postInit()`, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` is `null`. For the unknown shortcut "ac", `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` misses the map and dereferences `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, throwing a `NullPointerException`. Because the test catches the broad `RuntimeException`, it reports success while never exercising the intended `IllegalArgumentException("Unknown value 'ac' for grant type")` path. Catch `IllegalArgumentException` specifically (and assert its message), and make the fixture supply a non-null session factory so the refresh-on-miss code path is actually covered.

false_positives.candidate:
Access-token jti format change is not documented in release/upgrading notes

From this change on, every access token's `jti` (and the `token_id` event detail) is no longer a plain UUID but `<6 chars>:<uuid>`, e.g. `onrtac:1f65761e-...`. Relying parties that validate/store `jti` as a UUID (UUID columns, regex validation, replay caches keyed by UUID) will break, and no release note or upgrading guide entry is included in this PR. A user-visible format change of a standard claim needs an explicit documentation entry describing the new format and the fact that older tokens keep the plain-UUID form.

New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method on `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`, which is a documented extension point for custom grant types. Any third-party factory built against a previous release will fail to compile, and an already-built provider jar will fail at runtime with `AbstractMethodError` when `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories and calls `getShortcut()` — i.e. the whole server fails to start. Consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning the "unknown" shortcut) and handling it gracefully in the encoder factory, or at minimum document this as a breaking SPI change.

No validation of grant shortcut (null / wrong length) during postInit

`postInit()` puts `gtf.getShortcut()` directly into a `ConcurrentHashMap`. If a (third-party) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` returns `null`, `ConcurrentHashMap.put(null, ...)` throws a bare `NullPointerException` during `postInit`, aborting server startup with no indication of which provider is at fault. Similarly a shortcut whose length is not exactly 2 is accepted here but produces token ids that `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId()` rejects. Validate non-null and length==2 here with a message naming the offending factory, analogous to the existing duplicate-shortcut check.

Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) removed without deprecation

The `public Context(Context context)` copy constructor is deleted in this change. `OAuth2GrantType` is an extension SPI, so any external grant-type implementation that wrapped/copied the context (a natural pattern for decorating contexts) will no longer compile against this version. If removal is required because the new `grantType` field cannot be derived in a copy, either keep the constructor and copy `grantType` too, or state the removal explicitly in the upgrading notes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unguarded Optional.get() produces a 500 when the recovery-code credential cannot be read back

`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, but the bean immediately calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` (and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()`). With the new user-storage support, a provider can legitimately report `isConfiguredFor(recovery-authn-codes) == true` (so `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` shows the form) while exposing no credential object at all through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`/`getCredentials()` – that is exactly the default for any existing `CredentialInputUpdater` that does not implement credential listing. In that case the Optional is empty and rendering the login page throws `NoSuchElementException`, which surfaces as an internal server error instead of a login form. The bean should handle the empty case (e.g. fall back to code number 0 / a generic prompt) rather than dereferencing blindly.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recovery-code credential exposed by getCredentials() has no id

`updateCredential()` assigns `recoveryCodesModel.setId(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())`, but `getCredentials()` rebuilds the model with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...)`, which does not set an id, and the stored id is never copied over. Consumers of `getFederatedCredentialsStream()` therefore see a credential with `id == null`: the account console renders/deletes credentials by id, and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` calls `removeStoredCredentialById(model.getId())` with that null. The same bug was explicitly fixed for OTP in this diff (`newOTP.setId(...)`), so the recovery-code model should propagate the id too.

false_positives.candidate:
Login is never completed and logout result is ignored in testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin

Unlike the sibling tests, this test never calls `testAppHelper.completeLogin()` after submitting the recovery code, so the authorization code is never exchanged and no tokens (incl. the id/refresh token used by `TestAppHelper.logout()`) are obtained. The subsequent `testAppHelper.logout()` is then very likely a no-op/failure and its boolean result is discarded (other tests use `assertTrue(testAppHelper.logout())`). The result is that the test neither verifies a complete, token-producing login via a user-storage recovery code nor reliably tears the SSO session down, which can leak session state into the other tests in this class that log in as the same user `otp1`.

New user-storage credential contract for recovery codes is undocumented and asymmetric

`createRecoveryCodesCredential()` hands the user-storage provider a `UserCredentialModel` of type `recovery-authn-codes` whose value is a JSON array of all 12 *raw* codes, while validation (`UserCredentialModel.buildFromBackupAuthnCode()` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) hands the same provider a single raw code with dashes stripped. Nothing in the javadoc or in any SPI documentation states this format, that the codes arrive unhashed (so the provider is responsible for hashing them), or that the provider must mark a code consumed after a successful validation. Third-party providers implementing `CredentialInputUpdater.supportsCredentialType(recovery-authn-codes)` will silently store/compare the wrong thing. Please document the expected serialization and the one-time-use obligation on this method (and ideally use a stable constant instead of the hardcoded provider id "keycloak-recovery-authn-codes").

Recovery codes stored in the provider cannot be disabled/removed

`disableCredentialType()` only clears OTP and `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream()` only reports `CredentialModel.OTP`, yet `getCredentials()` now exposes the recovery-code credential to the account console and admin REST. The credential is therefore listed but there is no way to delete or disable it through the standard credential-management paths, which also means the new feature has no test for removing user-storage recovery codes (the OTP equivalent is covered by `testOTPSetupAndRemoveThroughAccountMgmtAndLogin`).

Reference provider never invalidates a used recovery code, so one-time-use is not covered by any test

`isValid()` for `recovery-authn-codes` simply checks whether the submitted value is contained in the stored plaintext list and returns true, without removing/marking the code as used. Consequently the same recovery code can be replayed an unlimited number of times against this provider, and the new integration test (`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin`) cannot detect that the critical one-time-use semantics of recovery codes are preserved when the credential lives in user storage. Please consume the code on successful validation (and add an assertion that re-using the same code fails, and that the next login asks for the following code number).

User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes go to user storage

The `UserCredentialModel` built here carries only the type and the JSON of the raw codes. The `credentialModel` argument, which holds the user-supplied label (`userLabel`) and the `generatedAt` timestamp collected by `RecoveryAuthnCodesAction`, is only used for its type on the user-storage path and is discarded. As a result a user who names their recovery-code set loses that label whenever the credential ends up in the user storage (the test provider indeed returns `getUserLabel() == null`), and the created date becomes the provider's own clock value rather than the generation time shown to the user.

getCredentials() NPEs for users not present in the provider map

`getCredentials()` does `var myUser = getMyUser(user); if (myUser.recoveryCodes != null)` with no null check, unlike every sibling method (`getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`, `isConfiguredFor`, `isValid`) which all guard against `getMyUser(user) == null`. Because this method is reached from `credentialManager().getFederatedCredentialsStream()` (account console credential listing, the new `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`), any call for a user id that is no longer in the in-memory map (removed user, stale cache entry, different factory instance) throws a NullPointerException out of the provider instead of returning an empty stream.

supportsCredentialType()/isConfiguredFor() can NPE on a null credential type

The new conditions are written as `credentialType.equals(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (lines 114 and 275), dereferencing the parameter. The pre-existing checks in the same expressions (`CredentialModel.PASSWORD.equals(credentialType)`, `isOTPType(...)`) are null-safe, so a null type used to be handled gracefully and now throws NullPointerException. Invert the comparison to `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE.equals(credentialType)`.

With a negative value, `range(self.num_processes)` is empty while `i % self.num_processes` still evaluates to 0, so the shard assignment loop raises `KeyError: 0` and the consumer crashes at startup with an opaque error. It is also subtly unsafe: if the shard is not found in `process_to_shards_map` it silently does nothing. Leaving it in invites a future caller to use the wrong restart path; delete it.

`_create_process_for_shards()` constructs a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process on every (re)start and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The class docstring now says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the `process-spans` consumer defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, i.e. a single process handling all shards. As a result `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown in the attributes tree by default and disappear only while the user is searching — the opposite of the intent, and visibly inconsistent behavior. `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba event lookup) followed by `event.get_environment()` (a DB/environment lookup) for every issue, and both GitHub and GitLab `get_comment_body` call it once per issue in a list comprehension. Consider resolving the environment in bulk (or from data already available on the group) instead of per-issue, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment, so these failures would be hard to notice.

The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails, so all other (valid) reports in the same POST are discarded and never counted. This is risky for a data-collection endpoint: the serializer requires `destination` and `attempts` (fields the Reporting API spec does not include in the delivered payload — browsers send `age`/`type`/`url`/`user_agent`/`body`) and restricts `type` to a fixed `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES` choice list, so newly introduced or spec-variant report types will now fail hard instead of being measured. `fieldAlignment(column.name, column.type as ColumnValueType)` passes the human-readable column label. When a caller supplies custom display names without an explicit `type` (the documented use case — e.g. `{key: 'count(span.duration)', name: 'Count of Span Duration'}` in the spec fixture), `fieldAlignment` falls back to name-based detection and cannot recognize the aggregate/numeric field, so numeric columns are left-aligned. For forward cursors a client-supplied negative offset is now silently clamped to 0 (returning page-one rows instead of surfacing an error for a malformed cursor), while for `is_prev` cursors the negative value is still passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, where Django raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` and the request 500s. The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect — the queryset rejects negative slices. Either validate the offset once and raise `BadPaginationError` (yielding a 400), or clamp in both branches; note also that the subsequent `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses the unclamped `offset`, so the two values can disagree.

The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` claims negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" enabling "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions". No validation was added or removed here, and negative offsets are not supported anywhere downstream: Django refuses negative slice starts (`ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.`) and the offset-based paginators explicitly raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Leaving this comment in a shared utility invites future callers to construct negative-offset cursors that will crash at query time; either remove the comment or add an explicit validation/rejection of negative offsets here.

A new public paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) and a new request-driven branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` are introduced without any tests. The behaviors that most need coverage are exactly those that are currently broken: a negative `cursor` offset with `optimized_pagination=true`, pagination with the `-datetime` sort key (which raises `TypeError` in `get_item_key`), and the permission gate when `organization_context.member` is `None`. Without tests these regressions reach production as 500s on a customer-facing endpoint.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` is a near-verbatim copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with one branch added, and it dropped the explanatory comments about the extra fetched row and the `post_query_filter` semantics. Any future fix to the base implementation (for example the offset clamping just added, or the `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` off-by-one when offset is clamped) has to be applied in two places and will silently diverge here. Override only the slicing step (e.g. a `_slice_bounds` hook) instead of copying the whole method.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex is no longer serialized per key, allowing duplicate/conflicting index creation

Previously `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole function, so two callers that both saw a cache miss in `getOrCreateIndex` were at least serialized. Now only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write is guarded. Two goroutines (e.g. the startup indexer and a `handleEvent`/`Search` triggered lazy build, or two search requests for the same namespace) can now build the same key concurrently: for the file-backed path both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory, which will fail for one of them (path already exists) or race on the on-disk index; for the memory path both succeed and the second write silently replaces the first in the cache. The replaced index is never `Close()`d, leaking memory/file handles, and any documents written to it (including watch events already applied) are lost. Consider a per-key lock or single-flight so only one build per key runs and the previous index is closed when replaced.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same concurrency bug in `BuildIndex` caused by moving the `cacheMu` lock to only protect the final cache assignment, allowing multiple goroutines to concurrently build the index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `cacheMu` from potentially many worker goroutines. A concurrent map read and map write is a fatal runtime error in Go (`concurrent map read and map write`), which would crash the process. This became reachable in a new place by this PR: `searchSupport.init` now logs `"total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs()`, and lazy builds triggered by watch events or search requests can still be writing the cache at that time. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` written from concurrent errgroup goroutines

Inside the `group.Go` closure the code does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and assigns to the function-scoped `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) instead of using local variables. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` and multiple namespaces these closures run in parallel, so both the counter increment and the `err` assignment are unsynchronized data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-report). Worse, the outer `err` is also the variable later checked after `group.Wait()` (`err = group.Wait()` overwrites it, but the races remain) and a build error written by one goroutine can be clobbered by another. Declare `err` locally in the closure and use an atomic counter.

Eager Init in the constructor blocks startup, ignores caller context, and turns transient failures into hard startup failures

`NewResourceServer` now runs the full initialization (lifecycle hook -> DB init, full search index build over every namespace, watcher start) synchronously and with the server's own `context.Background()`-derived context. Two consequences: (1) the caller cannot bound or cancel this work - there is no deadline, so the constructor can block for minutes while all indexes are built, delaying everything downstream of it in the wiring graph (including HTTP/readiness for the embedded single-binary mode); (2) any error (a single namespace failing to index, DB not yet reachable) now aborts construction and therefore process startup, whereas before the error was retried on the next request. At minimum the init should accept a caller-supplied context/timeout, and index building should not be a fatal startup error.

`Stop()` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped" and relies on every RPC calling `s.Init(ctx)` (which returns the cached `initErr`) to reject requests after shutdown. With all `s.Init(ctx)` calls removed from `Create`, `Update`, `Delete`, `Read`, `List`, `Watch`, `Search`, `History`, `Origin`, `IsHealthy`, `PutBlob` and `GetBlob`, requests arriving after `Stop()` now proceed and hit a canceled context / closed database, returning arbitrary internal errors instead of a clear "service is stopped". Either keep an explicit stopped-state check at the top of the handlers or document/remove the now-dead `initErr` assignments in `Stop`.

When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling the `cancel` created at line 229. The derived context is never canceled, and anything already started during the partially completed init (e.g. `initWatcher`'s broadcaster goroutine and the `WatchWriteEvents` poller goroutine, or the watch goroutine started inside `searchSupport.init` before a later error) keeps running for the lifetime of the process with no owner. The only integration test that exercises booting the `StorageServer` module is now skipped for postgres with the comment "test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally." Given that this PR moves unified-storage initialization into `NewResourceServer` (so module startup now performs DB init and full index building), a newly failing startup test for one database is exactly the signal that should be investigated rather than suppressed; skipping it leaves the eager-init path untested for postgres in CI and can hide a real startup regression (e.g. ordering versus migrations, or a timeout during index build).

This PR fixes the `_, span :=` pattern in `GetResourceStats`, `searchSupport.init` and `searchSupport.build`, but the same defect remains on the hot indexing path: `ListIterator` (line 388), `ReadResource` (line 353) and `WriteEvent` (line 158) start a span and then pass the original `ctx` to `listLatest`/`listAtRevision`/`create`/`update`/`delete`, so all the DB query spans attach to the caller's span instead of the `sql.resource.List`/`Read`/`WriteEvent` span. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:88) has the same issue. false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then silently drops all messages

`self.queue_pool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (line 133) and handed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo destroys and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/assignment, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every work queue. After the first rebalance a new strategy is created around the now-dead pool: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown` and every worker thread has exited. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` wraps everything in `except Exception` and then marks the offset as added+completed, those messages are never processed but their offsets are committed — i.e. total, silent data loss for the rest of the process lifetime. The pool must be owned by the strategy (recreated per assignment) or `shutdown()` must not be called from the strategy's close path.

submit() swallows every exception and marks the offset as completed, committing unprocessed messages

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception raised by the decoder, the grouping function, or `queue.put()` is caught by the blanket `except Exception`, logged, and then the offset is added and immediately completed so the commit loop will commit it. That means transient or structural failures (closed queue, grouping bug, OOM-adjacent errors, a `FilteredPayload` hitting the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`) result in the message being permanently skipped and its offset committed, with no DLQ and no retry. Only genuinely undecodable payloads should be fast-forwarded; everything else should propagate so arroyo can DLQ or crash the consumer.

Work queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and unbounded memory growth

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if one group's processing is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), arroyo will keep polling Kafka and the corresponding queue will grow without limit until the process OOMs. The problem is amplified because `WorkItem` also retains the whole `Message[KafkaPayload]` (line 31) even though only `partition`/`offset` are used, so each queued item holds the full Kafka payload alive. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or otherwise block) when full.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which is arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback mutates the `KafkaConsumer`'s staged-offset state and may call `commit_offsets()` while the main processor thread is concurrently polling and running rebalance callbacks (which also stage/commit offsets). This state is not lock-protected, and staging offsets for a partition that was just revoked raises `ConsumerError("cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions")`. That error is swallowed by the loop's broad `except Exception`, so commits can silently stop working after a rebalance while processing continues. Commits should be driven from `poll()`/the main thread instead of a separate thread.

close()/join() stop the commit thread before draining work, so completed work is never committed

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()` (which drains/stops workers). Any item processed after the last 1-second commit tick therefore has its offset marked complete but never committed, so it is reprocessed after restart. For uptime results this means duplicate processing of check results (duplicate status transitions/incidents) on every deploy. `join(timeout)` (line 344) also ignores its `timeout` argument and delegates to `close()`, which can block for up to ~5s per worker plus 5s for the commit thread, violating arroyo's shutdown deadline. A final `get_committable_offsets()` + `commit_function(..., force=True)` should run after the queues are drained.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued items are discarded despite immediate=False

`shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` with the intent of letting workers drain remaining items. But `OrderedQueueWorker.run` re-checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker processes at most one more item and exits; everything still queued is dropped. This makes the "gracefully shutdown" docstring wrong and means a shutdown under load discards all buffered work (it will be reprocessed, since those offsets stay outstanding, but the drain the code appears to implement never happens). Either drain first and set the flag afterwards, or use `shutdown(immediate=True)` and don't pretend to drain.

Worker marks offsets complete even when result processing raised, so failed messages are committed

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so a message whose `result_processor` raised an unexpected exception is logged and then its offset is committed. This silently converts processing failures into permanent message loss and diverges from the serial/batched modes, where an unhandled exception propagates to arroyo and can be DLQ'd or crash the consumer rather than being committed away. If skip-on-error is intended it should be explicit (and metered), not a side effect of `finally`.

OffsetTracker never cleans up revoked partitions and keeps stale last_committed values

`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed` and `partition_locks` grow per partition and are never pruned when partitions are revoked. Because the tracker lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, a partition that is revoked and later reassigned keeps its old `last_committed` value; if the consumer re-reads from a lower offset (normal after a rebalance), `get_committable_offsets` will refuse to commit anything for that partition until the stream passes the stale high-water mark, and the offsets below it are reprocessed without ever being committed. Add a way to drop per-partition state on revocation.

Every worker emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only `{"identifier": ...}` as tags, once per processed item. With N workers the samples overwrite each other (last writer wins) so the gauge reflects a random worker's queue rather than anything interpretable, while paying statsd overhead on every message. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or emit aggregate depth from `poll()` only (which already publishes `queue_pool.total_queued`).

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo internals that can change without notice), busy-loops for a hard-coded 5 seconds, and then asserts exact committed offsets. This makes the test slow and timing-dependent (a slow CI run that produces/consumes late will fail), and the `verify_consumer` is left unclosed if any assertion fails. Prefer the public `StreamProcessor.run()`/shutdown path or a condition-based wait with a generous timeout.

Redis value type change from SET to ZSET on the same key prefix breaks in-flight segments

`span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` keys are switched from plain Redis SETs (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`/`scard`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`/`zcard`) while keeping the exact same key names. Keys written by the previous code version live for `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), and during a rolling deploy old and new consumers write to the same keys. Any `ZADD`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZSCAN` against a key that is still a SET returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, which raises out of the pipeline in `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` and will crash-loop the consumer (or permanently fail those batches) until every legacy key expires. zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting span scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the identical span payload is a member of both source sorted sets — which happens with at-least-once Kafka redelivery where the same payload was first buffered under the parent key and later under the redirect-resolved set key — the resulting score becomes the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values (~2x epoch seconds). That span then sorts as the "newest" member forever, so the new `zpopmin` eviction will evict legitimate recent spans instead, and the score is no longer a meaningful timestamp. Please make the limit a script argument driven by `max_segment_spans` and return/emit an eviction count so the loss is observable.

Redirect-resolution loop limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000 and its warning comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. This 10x reduction means segment trees deeper than ~1000 redirects now stop resolving and get split into separate segments, which is a user-visible behaviour change unrelated to the stated purpose of this PR (insert-time eviction). Either keep the previous bound or document the new limit and the reason for lowering it.

The gate for the new pagination mode uses the raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag. In Sentry, holding the superuser flag is not the same as having an elevated/active superuser session; the supported check is `sentry.auth.superuser.is_active_superuser(request)` (or staff equivalent). Using the raw flag grants the privileged code path to any account with the flag set regardless of whether superuser mode was activated, bypassing the elevation requirement that the rest of the codebase enforces. Note also that `has_global_access` is true for every member of an open-membership organization, so the "authorized administrators" framing in the comment does not match what is actually checked.

Comment claims negative cursor offsets are a supported feature, which they are not

The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" for "efficient reverse pagination". Nothing in `Cursor` was changed, and the rest of the codebase explicitly rejects negative offsets (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator` all raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) while Django querysets raise `ValueError` on negative slices. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a validated, supported input.

max_segment_spans config is now dead code

`self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` is still set in `SpansBuffer.__init__` (default 1001) but the only consumer of it — the span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` — was deleted, and the new limit is hardcoded as `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect. Either thread the value into the Lua script as an ARGV or remove the constructor parameter.

The module docstring (steps 2-3 around line 38-39 and the glossary entry on line 58: "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes the span buffers as Redis sets and says the payload is added "to the set". They are now sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are evicted (oldest-first) once a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Since this docstring is the primary explanation of the buffer's Redis layout, it should document the new type and the lossy eviction behaviour.

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing while neighbouring optional fields use `val.get(...)`. Any message lacking the field (older producers, replayed/spillover topics, malformed payloads) raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the entire arroyo batch rather than a single message and will crash-loop the consumer on a poison message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly invalidating the single span.

All changes to `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`. Nothing exercises the new behaviour: no test pushes more than 1000 spans into a segment to verify that `zpopmin` trims to the limit, that the lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` spans are the ones evicted, that the root/segment span survives, or that merging two over-limit sub-segments via `zunionstore` still trims correctly. `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (~90 new lines, including a dedicated negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests at all. Basic coverage would have caught that `get_item_key` cannot handle the `datetime` field the endpoint orders by and that negative slice starts raise `ValueError` in Django. At minimum there should be tests for: the paginator with the endpoint's actual order_by, the permission gate (member=None, non-superuser, non-privileged member), and the rejection of negative offsets.

Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

Both recommend replacing `hash()` with a deterministic serialization of the sorted project IDs (such as joining them with commas). Even though the candidate also mentions additional concerns and emphasizes hash collisions alongside determinism, it directly identifies the exact same buggy code and proposes the exact same fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` as its first parameter and executes the query against it, but the eligibility check passes the enclosing `dataset` variable: `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)`. false_positives.candidate:
`upsampled_count` is only registered for the discover dataset but is applied to the errors dataset

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to `DiscoverDatasetConfig.function_converter` in `discover.py`. However `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform()` in `src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py` returns `True` unconditionally when `dataset is errors`, so for `?dataset=errors` requests the endpoint will send `upsampled_count() as count` to a builder backed by `ErrorsDatasetConfig`, which maintains its own independent `function_converter`. If that config does not also register `upsampled_count`, every errors-dataset timeseries request from an allowlisted project will fail with `InvalidSearchQuery: upsampled_count() is not a valid function` (HTTP 400) instead of returning data. Either register the function for the errors dataset config too, or restrict the transform to datasets that actually expose it. Note that the added tests only exercise the default (discover) dataset, so this path is completely uncovered.

Error-focus detection reads the raw request query instead of the query actually executed

`_is_error_focused_query()` inspects `request.GET["query"]`, but the query string that is actually executed is passed into `_get_event_stats` as the `query` argument and can differ from the request parameter. In the dashboard split path the endpoint builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (error-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transaction-only); both are evaluated using the same unmodified `request.GET["query"]`. So an error-only split query will not be upsampled unless the user happened to type `event.type:error`, and a transaction-only split query *will* be upsampled if the user's original query contained `event.type:error`, summing `sample_weight` over transactions where the column does not exist. The detection should operate on the query string handed to the dataset, not on the request parameter.

`sum(sample_weight)` silently returns 0 for events without a sample weight

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count()`, which is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. The docstring asserts "we rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists", but a project only gets a `sample_rate`/`sample_weight` once the SDK sends `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`; events ingested before upsampling was enabled, events from SDKs that do not send it, and events from other event sources in the same (allowlisted) project will have a NULL/0 weight. For those rows `sum(sample_weight)` contributes 0 instead of 1, so adding a project to the allowlist silently zeroes or undercounts historical and non-instrumented error counts in charts and alerts. The aggregate should fall back to 1 per row when `sample_weight` is absent (e.g. `sum(if(sample_weight > 0, sample_weight, 1))` or an equivalent coalesce).

`upsampled_count` is exposed as a public discover function

Unlike the neighbouring internal helper functions, the new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is not marked `private=True`, so any API consumer can request `field=upsampled_count()`/`yAxis=upsampled_count()` on discover/transaction queries. Since it compiles to `sum(sample_weight)` and `sample_weight` does not exist for transaction rows, this is a user-reachable path to a raw Snuba/ClickHouse "unknown column" error (500/snuba error surfaced to the client), and it becomes an unintentionally supported public API surface. Also, the aggregate returns `toInt64(...)` but declares `default_result_type="number"`; `"integer"` matches the actual value type and the result type reported for `count()`.

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` swallows all exceptions, hiding mis-set sample rates

Both the context lookup and the `float()` conversion are wrapped in bare `except Exception: pass`, and invalid/zero values are dropped by the `if client_sample_rate:` guard. If a test supplies a malformed `contexts.error_sampling.client_sample_rate`, `sample_rate` is silently not set and the stored event gets `sample_weight = 1`; the upsampling assertions (e.g. `count == 10`) then fail with no indication of why. Let the conversion raise (or assert) so test authors get an actionable error instead of a mysterious count mismatch.

No test covers the public entry point or its caching behaviour

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) and the column transform. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — the only function the endpoint actually calls, and the one containing the new 60s shared-cache logic — is never tested, nor is `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. As a result, the cache-hit path (including the `cached_result is not None` handling of a cached `False`, and the key-building logic duplicated between the two functions) is unverified, and regressions in the caching layer would silently change query results in production.

Accidental git submodule/gitlink `sentry-repo` committed

The PR adds a gitlink entry `sentry-repo` pointing at commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a (the PR's own base commit) with no corresponding `.gitmodules` entry. This is clearly a local workspace artifact: it makes `git submodule update`/`git clone --recurse-submodules` fail or warn about an uninitialized submodule with no URL, and pollutes the repo tree. It must be removed before merging.

`pyproject.toml` configures black/flake8 with `line-length = 100`, but the `cache_key` assignment on this line is ~110 characters, and the new file plus the edits in `organization_events_stats.py` contain trailing whitespace on several blank/comment lines (e.g. after `should_upsample = ...` and inside the docstrings). Pre-commit/black and flake8 will reject the diff as-is; run the formatter before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

`userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `action`, `name` and `parent` with `_` separators and no escaping, so distinct requests can produce the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="" and name="a", parent="b_" both yield `...<action>_a_b_`. Dashboard/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores and are user-chosen, so a crafted (or merely unlucky) pair of UIDs makes a cached denial for one resource deny access to an unrelated resource for up to the 30s TTL (availability/incorrect-deny, not escalation, since only denials are stored). The key also omits group/resource, relying on `action` to encode them. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions or include explicit length/field delimiters.

false_positives.candidate:
Every non-allowed Check now hits the database; denial cache is per (name, folder) and unbounded

The cache lookups were removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (a real `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` query) whenever the cached scope map does not already allow the request. The only protection against repeated queries is `permDenialCache`, whose key includes the resource name and parent folder (cache.go:30) and whose TTL is only 30s. Consequently a caller that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (object-by-object checks, or a client enumerating names) produces one uncached DB permission query per unique (action, name, folder) tuple, and fills the shared local cache with one entry per tuple (the authlib local cache has no size bound), so both DB load and memory are driven by caller-controlled input. This amplification is worse in-proc because the client-side cache was also disabled (rbac.go:103). Consider keeping a bounded/short-lived "permissions were just fetched" marker per (user, action) so the full re-query happens at most once per short interval rather than once per resource.

Stale folder tree still causes denials, and those denials are now cached

`Check` now re-queries permissions from the DB when the cached scope map does not allow the request, but `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still returns the cached folder tree (30s TTL) and is never refreshed when the requested parent folder is absent from it. So for a resource whose access is granted only through inheritance from an ancestor (e.g. a dashboard created in a brand-new subfolder of a folder the user has permissions on), the tree does not yet contain the new folder, the check denies, and the denial is then stored in `permDenialCache` (line 154), extending the window during which the user cannot see the newly created object. The stated goal of the PR (immediate access to newly created folders/dashboards) is therefore only met for directly-granted scopes. Consider re-fetching the folder tree (or at least not caching the denial) when `req.ParentFolder` is not present in the cached tree.

permissionCacheUsage metric is mislabelled on the new Check paths

In `Check`, a denial-cache hit increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="true"}` (line 118) even though the permission cache was not consulted at all, conflating two different caches in one metric. Conversely, when the permission cache *is* hit but the result is "not allowed", execution continues and line 137 increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="false"}`, reporting a cache miss for a request that was served from the cache. Cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts built on this metric will be wrong after this change; the denial cache should get its own metric and the hit label should reflect whether `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeded.

`permDenialKey` uses `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw value parsed from the subject, while `permCache` keys use the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID` (see `getCachedIdentityPermissions`/`getUserPermissions`). Because `GetUserIdentifiers` treats a numeric subject as a user ID, the same identity addressed as `user:1` and as `user:<uid>` gets two independent denial entries (wasted lookups/queries), and a user whose UID is literally a decimal number shares denial entries with the user whose internal ID equals that number, which can deny the wrong identity for the TTL. Resolve the identifiers first and build the denial key from `userIdentifiers.UID` for consistency.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

`OAuthLoginView` sends `state=pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates `request.GET["state"] == pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the fully-qualified class names of the pipeline views, i.e. a value that is identical for every user and every session (the new test even hard-codes it as `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). It is therefore not a per-session nonce and provides no CSRF/session binding: an attacker who authorizes the GitHub OAuth app themselves can hand a victim a URL such as `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known_signature>`.
