true_positives.reasoning: Although framed as a test-coverage issue, the candidate explicitly identifies the nil-content crash and unsanitized HTML path involving TopicEmbed.import, matching the golden comment's NoMethodError and XSS concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stray `if` in `<%- end if %>` corrupts the compiled template

The closing tag of the header conditional is written as `<%- end if %>` instead of `<%- end %>`. The extra `if` is compiled into Ruby as `end if <next emitted expression>`, i.e. the whole if/else block becomes the body of a modifier-`if` whose condition is whatever ERB happens to emit next (currently a whitespace `safe_append`). At best this works by accident and the header is rendered conditionally on an unrelated expression; a small change to surrounding whitespace/markup can turn it into a SyntaxError raised while rendering the embed page. Nothing catches this because controller specs do not render views (`render_views` is not enabled in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the stray `if` in `<%- end if %>` as the template bug and state that it should be `<%- end %>`. The candidate differs on the exact compilation behavior but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
poll_feed crashes on feed items without `content`

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item exposes a non-nil `content`. Plain RSS 2.0 feeds commonly only provide `description` (SimpleRSS exposes `content` only for Atom `content` / `content:encoded`), so `i.content` is nil and the job raises NoMethodError. Because the job is declared with `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the whole hourly poll aborts on the first such item and every remaining item in the feed is silently dropped. The same applies to `i.title`, which `TopicEmbed.import` passes to `PostCreator` as the topic title.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when RSS items lack content causes a nil-related exception. It also notes that these feeds commonly provide description instead, matching the golden comment's fallback concern. Additional observations do not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal and used as postMessage targetOrigin

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` injects a client-controlled header into inline JavaScript. ERB's HTML escaping does not apply to characters that matter inside a `<script>` block (a backslash is not escaped, and escaped entities are not decoded inside script elements), so a crafted Referer can break the surrounding string literal and produce a JS syntax error, and the full referer URL (path, query) is used where only an origin is meaningful. Derive the target origin from the validated host instead, e.g. `"#{uri.scheme}://#{uri.host}"` built from the parsed referer and JSON/JS-escaped.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unsafe interpolation of the client-controlled request.referer header into inline JavaScript and the need for JavaScript-specific escaping. Although it emphasizes string breakage and targetOrigin misuse rather than explicitly stating arbitrary script execution, the underlying injection concern matches the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed HTML is stored and rendered unsanitized (stored XSS)

`poll_feed` takes `i.content`, runs `CGI.unescapeHTML` on it (turning escaped markup back into live HTML) and passes it to `TopicEmbed.import`, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. `Post#cook` (app/models/post.rb:133) then returns `raw` verbatim, so the feed HTML is stored in `cooked` with no sanitization and is later emitted with `raw post.cooked` (app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19) and by the normal topic rendering. Any `<script>`, `onerror=`, or `javascript:` payload in the polled feed becomes persistent script execution on the forum for every visitor. The content should be run through the same whitelist/sanitizer used for `import_remote` (and `javascript:` hrefs stripped) before being trusted as raw HTML.

Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can permanently block retrieval of an embed URL

`$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)` is not atomic. If the process dies, the Redis connection drops, or the EXPIRE command fails between the two calls, the throttle key is left with no TTL and `retrieved_recently?` will return true forever for that embed URL, so the topic for that URL can never be retrieved again (the embed page will loop on the loading screen indefinitely). Use a single atomic command, e.g. `$redis.set(key, "1", ex: 60, nx: true)`.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

`href.start_with?('/')` is also true for protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. The rewrite then strips all leading slashes (`sub(/^\/+/, '')`) and prefixes the embed host, turning `//cdn.example.com/img.png` into `http://embedhost/cdn.example.com/img.png`, i.e. working absolute links/images in imported articles become broken links. The same bug applies to the `img` loop at lines 68-73. Protocol-relative URLs should be left alone (or only given a scheme), and relative URLs without a leading slash (`images/x.png`) are not handled at all — `URI.join` would handle all of these cases correctly.

TopicEmbed created from a post that may not have been saved; unique-index race unhandled

`creator.create` returns the (possibly unsaved) Post instance even when creation failed — PostCreator rolls back and returns `@post` carrying errors — so `post.present?` is true while `post.id` and `post.topic_id` are nil. `TopicEmbed.create!` then violates the NOT NULL constraints on `topic_id`/`post_id` and raises inside the job instead of failing gracefully; use `post.persisted?`. Additionally, `embed_url` has a unique index (db/migrate/20131217174004), and two concurrent retrievals for the same URL (the existence check in TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve is a plain read) will make one of them blow up with ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique; that case should be rescued and treated as "already imported".

`import` mutates the caller's contents string

`contents << "...imported_from..."` appends to the string object passed in by the caller rather than building a new string. Callers that reuse the string (or pass a frozen/literal string, which raises `RuntimeError: can't modify frozen String`) get surprising behaviour, and calling `import` twice with the same object appends the footer twice. Build a new string instead (`contents = contents + ...`).

New embed.css / embed.js assets are not added to the precompile list

The layout references `stylesheet_link_tag 'embed'` and the whole feature depends on third-party sites loading `embed.js` directly, but neither `embed.css` nor `embed.js` is a Sprockets entry point reachable from `application.js`/`application.css`, and this PR does not add them to `config.assets.precompile` (config/application.rb is untouched). In production with asset digests/compilation this raises `Asset was not declared to be precompiled in production` when the embed page is rendered and `embed.js` will 404 for embedding sites.

"is 404 without an embed_url" passes for the wrong reason

This example does not stub `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, so the `ensure_embeddable` before_filter raises `Discourse::InvalidAccess('embeddable host not set')` before `params.require(:embed_url)` is ever reached. The test therefore asserts nothing about the missing-parameter behaviour (and would keep passing if `params.require` were removed). It should stub `embeddable_host` and a matching referer, and assert the actual expected status. There is also no example covering a referer whose host differs from `embeddable_host` — the main security check of this controller.

Line 110 compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is a UTC dayjs object, but `dayjs(date.start)` is in the process-local timezone, so `.format()` renders the override date in whatever `TZ` the server runs with. On a server that is not UTC, overrides whose converted instant lies near midnight UTC will be compared against a different calendar day, so the override is silently not detected (falling through to the normal working-hours path) or matched on the wrong day. The new override conversion (lines 216-224) computes minutes-since-midnight as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. When the timezone shift moves the override across midnight (e.g. organizer 10:00-11:00 in Asia/Kolkata viewed by an America/Los_Angeles invitee, offset = -750 min), the converted instant lands on the previous day but only hour/minute are kept, so the override is interpreted as 21:30-22:30 of the invitee's current day — roughly 24 hours away from the real time. The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events, but the only new assertion (lines 788-804) re-queries a single-user event type with Asia/Dhaka. There is no scenario with a round-robin event type having a fixed host with a date override plus an available round-robin host, so the new `checkIfIsAvailable` override/working-hours path is untested for the case it was written for. In addition, both tested timezones are east of the organizer's (+5:30 and +6:00, a 30-minute shift), so the day-rollover case (an invitee timezone west of the organizer, e.g. America/Los_Angeles) — which is where the override conversion in packages/lib/slots.ts breaks — is not covered.

updateLocation writes references with an always-undefined externalCalendarId

`externalCalendarId: result.externalId` is used for the references created by `updateLocation()`, but `updateEvent()` in `packages/core/CalendarManager.ts` never sets `externalId` on its returned `EventResult` (only `createEvent` does). So `result.externalId` is always `undefined` here and the new `BookingReference` rows lose the external calendar id that was previously taken from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Later cancel/reschedule flows that rely on `reference.externalCalendarId` will then fall back to the provider's primary calendar and fail to find the event.

Destination calendars without credentialId lose their externalId in references and events

In `createAllCalendarEvents`, the branch for a destination without `credentialId` calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing `destination.externalId`. Because `EventResult.externalId` is what now populates `referencesToCreate.externalCalendarId` (see line 169), those bookings get references with no external calendar id. Combined with the Google service now resolving the target calendar by `credentialId` match only, such events are also created in `"primary"` instead of the configured destination calendar. Previously `evt.destinationCalendar.externalId` was used for both the reference and the target calendar.

updateAllCalendarEvents failures are now silently swallowed

The `console.error(message)` call was removed from the catch block, but `message` is still built from the error. Any failure while updating calendar events (including an `undefined` credential being passed to `updateEvent`) now returns fake failed results with no log line at all, making production diagnosis of calendar update failures impossible.

deleteEvent always falls back to 'primary' calendar

Same dead-condition as in `updateEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it always yields `undefined` and `calendarId` becomes `defaultCalendarId` (`"primary"`). Previously the destination calendar's `externalId` was used. Cancellations for bookings stored in a non-primary Google calendar will now hit the primary calendar, return 404 (swallowed as success) and leave the real event in place.

events.patch is called with a possibly undefined calendarId

`selectedCalendar` can now be `undefined` (the `|| "primary"` default was only applied inline at the `events.insert` call). The follow-up `calendar.events.patch({ calendarId: selectedCalendar, ... })` that writes the hangout link into the description still uses the raw value, producing a malformed request URL when no destination calendar matches the credential. The promise is not awaited or caught, so this fails silently and the Meet link is missing from the event description.

createEvent target calendar now resolved only by credentialId match

`calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId` replaces the former `calEventRaw.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. `DestinationCalendar.credentialId` is nullable, and `EventManager` reaches this service via the no-credentialId branch for such rows (passing no credential match), so for every destination calendar with a null `credentialId` the event is now created in `"primary"` instead of the user-selected calendar — a silent regression for existing single-host setups.

CalDAV createEvent reports success while creating nothing for secondary hosts

`EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` now iterates every destination calendar and calls `createEvent` with that host's credential, but this service still filters the account's calendars against `destinationCalendar[0]` (the main host). When invoked with a second host's credential, no calendar URL matches, `responses` is an empty array, `responses.some((r) => !r.ok)` is false, and the method returns a success result with a fresh uid even though no event was created on any calendar. The booking reference is stored and the host never gets the event, with no error surfaced.

Office365 createEvent always uses the first host's calendar id

Only `destinationCalendar[0]` is honoured. With the new multi-destination flow, `EventManager` calls `createEvent` once per destination using that destination's owner credential; for the second host this builds `/me/calendars/<first host's calendar id>/events` while authenticating as the second host, which 404s (or writes to the wrong calendar if ids happen to collide). The service should select the destination matching the credential it was constructed with (as the Google service now does via the new `credentialId` argument).

Lark createEvent/createAttendees always use the first host's calendar

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []` is used for the calendar id in `createEvent`, `createAttendees`, `updateEvent` and `deleteEvent`. Since `EventManager` now invokes these once per destination calendar with the corresponding host's credential, every host's run targets the first host's calendar id, producing duplicate events on the main host's calendar (or API errors) and no event on the other hosts' calendars.

Collective team destination calendars are dropped when no primary destination exists

`evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` uses optional chaining, but `destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. In that case the collected co-host destination calendars are silently discarded and the very bug this PR targets (collective hosts not getting calendar events) remains for teams whose organizer has no destination calendar. Initialise the array (e.g. `[]`) before pushing.

organization relation dropped from the dynamic-booking user select

The rewritten `loadUsers` removes `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the `prisma.user.findMany` select used for dynamic (no eventTypeId) bookings, while the host-based branch keeps whatever the event type query selected. Any downstream use of `user.organization` for dynamic group bookings now sees `undefined` (and the two branches no longer return the same shape, so the inferred union type changes). This change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar fix and should be reverted unless the field is provably unused.

Recurring cancellation deletes every event once per calendar reference

The recurring/`allRemainingBookings` block, which already loops over all of the user's calendar credentials and all updated bookings, is now nested inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references the same delete calls are issued N times (N × credentials × bookings), multiplying provider API calls and rate-limit risk; the outer `calendar` instance created from `calendarCredential` is also unused in that branch. The recurring branch should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

Webhook/CalendarEvent payload shape changed from object to array without versioning

`destinationCalendar` changes from `DestinationCalendar | null` to `DestinationCalendar[] | null`. This field is forwarded verbatim to webhook subscribers via `sendPayload` (see the e2e expectations, which now mix `destinationCalendar: null` for BOOKING_CREATED/REQUESTED and `[]` for BOOKING_REJECTED). External consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` will break, and the payload is now inconsistent (`null` vs `[]` vs array) depending on the code path. The shape should be normalised and the breaking payload change documented.

No tests for the new multi-destination calendar fan-out

`createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` now loop over an array of destination calendars, fetch foreign credentials from the DB and build one reference per created event, and every provider service was touched. The only test change in the PR is flipping one e2e expectation from `null` to `[]`. There is no unit/integration coverage asserting that a collective event with two hosts creates exactly one event per host calendar, that references carry the right `credentialId`/`externalCalendarId`, or that the single-host fallback is unchanged — all of which the findings above show are currently broken for several providers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected app-import promises are created with no handler attached (unhandled rejection at startup)

Each value in `appStore` is a promise created at module load and stored for an indefinite amount of time before any consumer awaits it. If any one app module fails to evaluate (missing/incorrect peer dependency, module-scope code that throws, bad env configuration), the corresponding promise rejects with no `.catch()` attached, producing an unhandled promise rejection at process start — which terminates the Node process on Node >= 15. Previously a broken app module failed loudly and synchronously at import time with a clear stack trace; now it can either kill the server or silently surface later as a generic "Could not get connected calendars" error from `getConnectedCalendars`'s catch block. Promises for apps that are never used are never awaited at all, so their rejections are always unhandled.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag missing error handling for asynchronous app imports and the need to handle rejected import promises gracefully. The candidate adds startup timing and unhandled-rejection consequences, but identifies the same underlying concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves deletions unawaited

The loop was changed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); … })`. The enclosing `try { … } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can never observe errors thrown inside an async callback, so the explicit error logging is dead code and failures surface as unhandled promise rejections. The function also continues to send the reschedule email and return `true` before the awaited dynamic app import resolves, so the calendar/video cancellations are fire-and-forget and may not run to completion in a short-lived (serverless) process. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))` so the try/catch works and the work is actually awaited.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify async callbacks passed to forEach as unawaited fire-and-forget operations, causing unhandled rejections, ineffective surrounding try/catch, and potentially incomplete cleanup. The candidate also recommends the same Promise.all with map remedy.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are started eagerly, so nothing is actually lazily loaded

`appStore` is now an object literal whose values are the *results* of calling `import("./app")` at module-evaluation time. Calling `import()` immediately starts loading the module, so every single app package (applecalendar, googlecalendar, stripepayment, …) is still pulled in as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is imported — the only thing that changed is that consumers now have to `await` the already in-flight promise. The PR's goal of async/lazy app loading is not achieved, while the extra `async`/`await` plumbing added across CalendarManager, videoClient, handleCancelBooking, bookings.tsx etc. buys nothing. To actually defer loading, the map must hold thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and call sites must invoke them, e.g. `await appStore[key]()`.

Example comment points at a non-existent path

The template comment was changed from `// import * as example from "./_example";` to `// example: import("./example"),`. The example app lives in the `_example` directory, so anyone uncommenting/copying this line will get a module-not-found error. The commented path should be `./_example`.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in the `calendar` field, changing its public contract

`getCalendarCredentials` is exported and returns `{ integration, credential, calendar }`. Because `getCalendar` became async, `calendar` is now `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other caller that reads `.calendar` keeps a promise, which is always truthy, so guards like `if (!calendar)` silently pass and subsequent `calendar.listCalendars()` style calls fail at runtime. Additionally, these promises are created eagerly for every credential inside a non-async function, so if a caller only needs `integration`/`credential`, a rejected `getCalendar` promise is never handled. Either make the function async and await the calendars, or keep the field lazy (a thunk) and update all consumers.

requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events in an unawaited forEach(async) callback

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) })` is not awaited, so the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule-request email, fire webhooks and return before the deletions are even initiated. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so the `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` requests were at least started before the handler continued; now the first thing the callback does is await a dynamic module import, meaning in a serverless/edge runtime the function can be frozen or torn down after the response and the stale calendar entries / video meetings will never be removed. Rejections are also unobserved (unhandled promise rejection). Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))` or a `for … of` loop.

forEach(async) makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves deletions unawaited

Same problem as in the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); … })` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that can no longer catch anything, because errors raised inside the async callbacks reject the (discarded) returned promises instead of propagating synchronously — they become unhandled promise rejections. Additionally the booking is marked cancelled and the reschedule email is sent before the awaited dynamic app import resolves, so the external calendar/video cancellation requests may never be issued. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => …))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key and high-cardinality tag value for shard groups

The produce timer and segment size metrics are tagged `{"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195) while the wait_produce timer is tagged `{"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199) — two different tag keys for the same dimension, which will silently split dashboards/queries. Worse, `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of all shards owned by the process (e.g. `"0,3,6"`), whose value depends on the Kafka partition assignment of each consumer instance and changes on every rebalance. `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` is emitted per segment, so this adds a per-assignment, unbounded-cardinality tag to a very high-volume metric. Use a single stable tag key and either omit the shard tag or emit one metric per concrete shard.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: produce/segment_size metrics use tag key 'shard' while wait_produce uses 'shards' for the same shard dimension, causing dashboards and queries to split. The additional high-cardinality concern does not change the underlying issue match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

Line 15 does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `time.sleep` globally for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62, whose comment claims to "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore returns immediately and provides no synchronisation at all. The test still races: if the flusher thread has not observed the new `current_drift` before `step.join()` sets `stopped`, `messages` stays empty and `(msg,) = messages` fails with a ValueError. Either use a real sleep (e.g. capture the original `time.sleep` before patching) or poll on `messages` with a timeout.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in test_basic: the monkeypatched time.sleep returns immediately, so the later time.sleep(0.1) provides no real wait and the test can race.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is always False for spawn processes, so unhealthy flushers are never killed

`self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")` creates processes of type `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`, which is *not* a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process` (that name resolves to `multiprocessing.context.Process` of the default context). Therefore the guard `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.kill()` never fires, and the previous unconditional `self.process.kill()` behaviour is lost. Consequence: when a flusher is declared unhealthy (hang or non-responsive), the old OS process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards()` immediately starts a second process for the *same* shards. Two processes then call `flush_segments()`/`done_flush_segments()` on the same Redis shards, which can produce duplicated segments to `buffered-segments` and leaks a process on every restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per shard group). The same wrong check is used in `join()` (line 346), so `terminate()` is also never called on shutdown. Use `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess instances, not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance guard never triggers and hung flushers are not killed. The candidate adds extra consequences and a suggested fix, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() abandons remaining processes once the deadline expires

In `join()`, the per-process loop computes `remaining_time` only to `break` out of the whole loop when the deadline has passed. Processes later in the iteration order are then neither waited on nor terminated, so on a timed-out shutdown an arbitrary subset of flusher processes is left running (they are daemons, so they die only when the parent exits). The computed `remaining_time` is otherwise unused — the inner wait loop re-checks `deadline` instead, so the first process can consume the entire timeout. Terminate every process regardless of the deadline.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same shutdown bug: when the deadline expires, join() breaks out of the per-process loop and skips waiting on/terminating later flusher processes, leaving them running. The candidate adds extra detail but points to the same underlying issue and fix.

false_positives.candidate:
No validation of flusher_processes; negative value raises KeyError, 0 silently means one process per shard

`--flusher-processes` is parsed as a plain int with no range validation and is used as `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` / `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`. With `--flusher-processes 0`, `0 or N` evaluates to `N`, so the operator silently gets one process per assigned shard instead of the obvious interpretation. With a negative value, `range(self.num_processes)` is empty while `i % self.num_processes` still evaluates to 0, so the shard assignment loop raises `KeyError: 0` and the consumer crashes at startup with an opaque error. Validate the option (>= 1) in the click option or in `__init__`.

New flusher test asserts a tautology and never exercises the multiprocess path

`total_shards = sum(len(shards) for shards in flusher.process_to_shards_map.values()); assert total_shards == 4` is trivially satisfied by the construction loop and would still pass if a shard were assigned twice while another was dropped. The meaningful invariant — that the union of `process_to_shards_map` values equals the assigned shards exactly once each — is not checked. In addition, because `produce_to_pipe` is passed, `SpanFlusher` takes the `threading.Thread` branch, so the test does not cover the actual `SpawnProcess` path this PR introduces (process creation, pickling of the per-shard `SpansBuffer`, restart/kill logic), and the factory is never shut down (`fac.shutdown()` is not called).

Dead method _create_process_for_shard is unused and silently no-ops for unknown shards

`_create_process_for_shard(shard)` has no callers anywhere after the refactor (health checking now goes through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). It is also subtly unsafe: if the shard is not found in `process_to_shards_map` it silently does nothing. Leaving it in invites a future caller to use the wrong restart path; delete it.

Parent-side SpansBuffer per process is replaced on restart without closing the old one

`_create_process_for_shards()` constructs a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` in the parent process on every (re)start and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent uses these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so they hold live Redis connections; the overwritten buffer is never closed, so each flusher restart leaks the old buffer's Redis client(s) in the main consumer process until GC. Note also that the `buffer` argument passed to `SpanFlusher` is now used only for `assigned_shards` — the extra parent-side buffers duplicate the Redis clients already held by the span-writing buffer.

Docstring claims one process per shard and omits the new max_processes parameter

The class docstring now says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the actual behaviour is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes, and the `process-spans` consumer defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, i.e. a single process handling all shards. The docstring's parameter list documents `topic` (which is not a parameter) and `produce_to_pipe`, but not the new `max_processes` argument or its `None` default (one process per shard). This will mislead operators tuning the flusher.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs error IDs with nodestore values by dict order

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics recorded before the feature check and payload validation

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs at the top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature gate and before schema validation. Every probe/404 and every malformed request is therefore counted as an assemble call, which makes the metric unusable for measuring real usage. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: analytics.record runs before the feature-flag gate, so disabled/404 requests are counted and distort metrics. The candidate additionally mentions schema validation, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Error/breadcrumb interleaving compares seconds against milliseconds

`gen_request_data` orders errors relative to replay events with `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data, which is a Unix timestamp in seconds (~1.7e9), while rrweb recording events carry `timestamp` as epoch milliseconds (~1.7e12). Every error will therefore compare as "earlier" than every breadcrumb and all error log lines will be emitted before any breadcrumb, destroying the chronological context the feature is built to provide. The new tests don't catch this because the fixtures build segment events with second-resolution timestamps; please normalize units (and add a test with realistic millisecond rrweb timestamps).

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter is skipped unless a search query is typed

`sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `searchQuery` is empty, and only applies the `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` filter in the search branch. As a result `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are shown in the attributes tree by default and disappear only while the user is searching — the opposite of the intent, and visibly inconsistent behavior. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied to the base list before the search short-circuit.

get_environment_info issues a Snuba + DB query per issue inside comment generation

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` (a Snuba event lookup) followed by `event.get_environment()` (a DB/environment lookup) for every issue, and both GitHub and GitLab `get_comment_body` call it once per issue in a list comprehension. That adds up to 5 extra Snuba queries plus environment fetches per PR/MR comment, on a path that previously only used already-loaded `Group` fields. Consider resolving the environment in bulk (or from data already available on the group) instead of per-issue, and note that the broad `except Exception` silently degrades to no environment, so these failures would be hard to notice.

One nonconforming report causes the entire batch to be dropped with 422

The loop validates each report and returns `422` for the whole request as soon as any single report fails, so all other (valid) reports in the same POST are discarded and never counted. This is risky for a data-collection endpoint: the serializer requires `destination` and `attempts` (fields the Reporting API spec does not include in the delivered payload — browsers send `age`/`type`/`url`/`user_agent`/`body`) and restricts `type` to a fixed `BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES` choice list, so newly introduced or spec-variant report types will now fail hard instead of being measured. Prefer validating per report and skipping/counting invalid ones (with a metric/log) while still returning 200 for the rest.

`TableWidgetVisualization`'s prop docs (and the story) state that returning `undefined` from `renderTableBodyCell`/`renderTableHeadCell` falls back to the default renderer, but the implementation checks `if (cell)`. If the deadline is hit the task is killed, but `check_auth` has already bumped `last_synced` for the whole batch, so the unprocessed identities will not be re-selected until the next ~24h cutoff and their SSO validity silently goes unchecked. Either raise the deadline, lower the default chunk size, or only update `last_synced` after an identity is actually processed.

Additionally, after reporting the mismatch the method `break`s and leaves the remaining `<a>` tags in the value, so the subsequent policy check emits a second, redundant "Illegal HTML" message for the same key.

HTML detection in the English source only recognises lower-case tags `HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` is case sensitive, so an English source value written with an upper-case tag (e.g. `` or `

Previously `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` held `cacheMu` for the whole function, so two callers that both saw a cache miss in `getOrCreateIndex` were at least serialized. Now only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write is guarded. Two goroutines (e.g. the startup indexer and a `handleEvent`/`Search` triggered lazy build, or two search requests for the same namespace) can now build the same key concurrently: for the file-backed path both call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory, which will fail for one of them (path already exists) or race on the on-disk index; for the memory path both succeed and the second write silently replaces the first in the cache. The replaced index is never `Close()`d, leaking memory/file handles, and any documents written to it (including watch events already applied) are lost. Consider a per-key lock or single-flight so only one build per key runs and the previous index is closed when replaced.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

This became reachable in a new place by this PR: `searchSupport.init` now logs `"total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs()`, and lazy builds triggered by watch events or search requests can still be writing the cache at that time. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` and multiple namespaces these closures run in parallel, so both the counter increment and the `err` assignment are unsynchronized data races (detectable by `-race`, and the counter will under-report). Worse, the outer `err` is also the variable later checked after `group.Wait()` (`err = group.Wait()` overwrites it, but the races remain) and a build error written by one goroutine can be clobbered by another. Declare `err` locally in the closure and use an atomic counter.

Two consequences: (1) the caller cannot bound or cancel this work - there is no deadline, so the constructor can block for minutes while all indexes are built, delaying everything downstream of it in the wiring graph (including HTTP/readiness for the embedded single-binary mode); (2) any error (a single namespace failing to index, DB not yet reachable) now aborts construction and therefore process startup, whereas before the error was retried on the next request. `Stop()` sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped" and relies on every RPC calling `s.Init(ctx)` (which returns the cached `initErr`) to reject requests after shutdown. false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on the first rebalance, then silently drops all messages

`self.queue_pool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (line 133) and handed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` created by `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo destroys and recreates the processing strategy on every partition revocation/assignment, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` on all workers and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every work queue. After the first rebalance a new strategy is created around the now-dead pool: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown` and every worker thread has exited. Because `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` wraps everything in `except Exception` and then marks the offset as added+completed, those messages are never processed but their offsets are committed — i.e. total, silent data loss for the rest of the process lifetime. The pool must be owned by the strategy (recreated per assignment) or `shutdown()` must not be called from the strategy's close path.

submit() swallows every exception and marks the offset as completed, committing unprocessed messages

In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception raised by the decoder, the grouping function, or `queue.put()` is caught by the blanket `except Exception`, logged, and then the offset is added and immediately completed so the commit loop will commit it. That means transient or structural failures (closed queue, grouping bug, OOM-adjacent errors, a `FilteredPayload` hitting the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`) result in the message being permanently skipped and its offset committed, with no DLQ and no retry. Only genuinely undecodable payloads should be fast-forwarded; everything else should propagate so arroyo can DLQ or crash the consumer.

Work queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and unbounded memory growth

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`. The class docstring claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but nothing ever fills up: if one group's processing is slow (the exact scenario this PR targets), arroyo will keep polling Kafka and the corresponding queue will grow without limit until the process OOMs. The problem is amplified because `WorkItem` also retains the whole `Message[KafkaPayload]` (line 31) even though only `partition`/`offset` are used, so each queued item holds the full Kafka payload alive. Give the queues a bounded size and raise `MessageRejected` (or otherwise block) when full.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded contract

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(...)`, which is arroyo's `StreamProcessor` commit callback. That callback mutates the `KafkaConsumer`'s staged-offset state and may call `commit_offsets()` while the main processor thread is concurrently polling and running rebalance callbacks (which also stage/commit offsets). This state is not lock-protected, and staging offsets for a partition that was just revoked raises `ConsumerError("cannot stage offsets for unassigned partitions")`. That error is swallowed by the loop's broad `except Exception`, so commits can silently stop working after a rebalance while processing continues. Commits should be driven from `poll()`/the main thread instead of a separate thread.

close()/join() stop the commit thread before draining work, so completed work is never committed

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()` (which drains/stops workers). Any item processed after the last 1-second commit tick therefore has its offset marked complete but never committed, so it is reprocessed after restart. For uptime results this means duplicate processing of check results (duplicate status transitions/incidents) on every deploy. `join(timeout)` (line 344) also ignores its `timeout` argument and delegates to `close()`, which can block for up to ~5s per worker plus 5s for the commit thread, violating arroyo's shutdown deadline. A final `get_committable_offsets()` + `commit_function(..., force=True)` should run after the queues are drained.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued items are discarded despite immediate=False

`shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` with the intent of letting workers drain remaining items. But `OrderedQueueWorker.run` re-checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker processes at most one more item and exits; everything still queued is dropped. This makes the "gracefully shutdown" docstring wrong and means a shutdown under load discards all buffered work (it will be reprocessed, since those offsets stay outstanding, but the drain the code appears to implement never happens). Either drain first and set the flag afterwards, or use `shutdown(immediate=True)` and don't pretend to drain.

Worker marks offsets complete even when result processing raised, so failed messages are committed

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally` block, so a message whose `result_processor` raised an unexpected exception is logged and then its offset is committed. This silently converts processing failures into permanent message loss and diverges from the serial/batched modes, where an unhandled exception propagates to arroyo and can be DLQ'd or crash the consumer rather than being committed away. If skip-on-error is intended it should be explicit (and metered), not a side effect of `finally`.

OffsetTracker never cleans up revoked partitions and keeps stale last_committed values

`all_offsets`, `outstanding`, `last_committed` and `partition_locks` grow per partition and are never pruned when partitions are revoked. Because the tracker lives on the long-lived `FixedQueuePool`, a partition that is revoked and later reassigned keeps its old `last_committed` value; if the consumer re-reads from a lower offset (normal after a rebalance), `get_committable_offsets` will refuse to commit anything for that partition until the stream passes the stale high-water mark, and the offsets below it are reprocessed without ever being committed. Add a way to drop per-partition state on revocation.

Per-item queue_depth gauge is emitted by all workers with identical tags, making the metric meaningless

Every worker emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only `{"identifier": ...}` as tags, once per processed item. With N workers the samples overwrite each other (last writer wins) so the gauge reflects a random worker's queue rather than anything interpretable, while paying statsd overhead on every message. Either tag by `worker_id`/queue index or emit aggregate depth from `poll()` only (which already publishes `queue_pool.total_queued`).

Kafka integration test relies on private arroyo APIs and a fixed 5-second wall-clock loop

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` drives the consumer by calling `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private arroyo internals that can change without notice), busy-loops for a hard-coded 5 seconds, and then asserts exact committed offsets. This makes the test slow and timing-dependent (a slow CI run that produces/consumes late will fail), and the `verify_consumer` is left unclosed if any assertion fails. Prefer the public `StreamProcessor.run()`/shutdown path or a condition-based wait with a generous timeout.

false_positives.candidate:
Redis value type change from SET to ZSET on the same key prefix breaks in-flight segments

`span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` keys are switched from plain Redis SETs (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`/`scard`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`/`zcard`) while keeping the exact same key names. Keys written by the previous code version live for `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), and during a rolling deploy old and new consumers write to the same keys. Any `ZADD`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZSCAN` against a key that is still a SET returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, which raises out of the pipeline in `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` and will crash-loop the consumer (or permanently fail those batches) until every legacy key expires. The key prefix needs to be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) or the data explicitly migrated/flushed as part of the rollout.

zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting span scores on duplicate payloads

`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the identical span payload is a member of both source sorted sets — which happens with at-least-once Kafka redelivery where the same payload was first buffered under the parent key and later under the redirect-resolved set key — the resulting score becomes the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values (~2x epoch seconds). That span then sorts as the "newest" member forever, so the new `zpopmin` eviction will evict legitimate recent spans instead, and the score is no longer a meaningful timestamp. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) explicitly.

Eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans with no metric or log

The new trimming logic hardcodes `span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000`, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) which is now never used, so the limit is neither configurable nor consistent with the Python config. In addition, the previous behaviour emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and an error log when a segment exceeded the span count; now spans are dropped silently inside Lua, so there is no metric, log, or dashboard signal that data loss occurred. Please make the limit a script argument driven by `max_segment_spans` and return/emit an eviction count so the loss is observable.

Redirect-resolution loop limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000 and its warning comment deleted

The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. This 10x reduction means segment trees deeper than ~1000 redirects now stop resolving and get split into separate segments, which is a user-visible behaviour change unrelated to the stated purpose of this PR (insert-time eviction). Either keep the previous bound or document the new limit and the reason for lowering it.

Superuser check uses request.user.is_superuser instead of is_active_superuser(request)

The gate for the new pagination mode uses the raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag. In Sentry, holding the superuser flag is not the same as having an elevated/active superuser session; the supported check is `sentry.auth.superuser.is_active_superuser(request)` (or staff equivalent). Using the raw flag grants the privileged code path to any account with the flag set regardless of whether superuser mode was activated, bypassing the elevation requirement that the rest of the codebase enforces. Note also that `has_global_access` is true for every member of an open-membership organization, so the "authorized administrators" framing in the comment does not match what is actually checked.

Comment claims negative cursor offsets are a supported feature, which they are not

The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" for "efficient reverse pagination". Nothing in `Cursor` was changed, and the rest of the codebase explicitly rejects negative offsets (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator` all raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) while Django querysets raise `ValueError` on negative slices. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a validated, supported input.

max_segment_spans config is now dead code

`self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` is still set in `SpansBuffer.__init__` (default 1001) but the only consumer of it — the span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` — was deleted, and the new limit is hardcoded as `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect. Either thread the value into the Lua script as an ARGV or remove the constructor parameter.

Module docstring still describes plain sets and omits insert-time eviction

The module docstring (steps 2-3 around line 38-39 and the glossary entry on line 58: "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes the span buffers as Redis sets and says the payload is added "to the set". They are now sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are evicted (oldest-first) once a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Since this docstring is the primary explanation of the buffer's Redis layout, it should document the new type and the lossy eviction behaviour.

Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can hard-fail a whole batch

`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing while neighbouring optional fields use `val.get(...)`. Any message lacking the field (older producers, replayed/spillover topics, malformed payloads) raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the entire arroyo batch rather than a single message and will crash-loop the consumer on a poison message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly invalidating the single span.

No test for the new insert-time eviction, the headline change of this PR

All changes to `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`. Nothing exercises the new behaviour: no test pushes more than 1000 spans into a segment to verify that `zpopmin` trims to the limit, that the lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` spans are the ones evicted, that the root/segment span survives, or that merging two over-limit sub-segments via `zunionstore` still trims correctly. The eviction path (and the score-based ordering it depends on) is therefore completely untested.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit-log code path have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (~90 new lines, including a dedicated negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests at all. Basic coverage would have caught that `get_item_key` cannot handle the `datetime` field the endpoint orders by and that negative slice starts raise `ValueError` in Django. At minimum there should be tests for: the paginator with the endpoint's actual order_by, the permission gate (member=None, non-superuser, non-privileged member), and the rejection of negative offsets.

`upsampled_count` is only registered for the discover dataset but is applied to the errors dataset

In the dashboard split path the endpoint builds `f"({query}) AND !event.type:transaction"` (error-only) and `f"({query}) AND event.type:transaction"` (transaction-only); both are evaluated using the same unmodified `request.GET["query"]`. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. true_positives.matched_candidate:

`userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `action`, `name` and `parent` with `_` separators and no escaping, so distinct requests can produce the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="" and name="a", parent="b_" both yield `...<action>_a_b_`. Dashboard/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores and are user-chosen, so a crafted (or merely unlucky) pair of UIDs makes a cached denial for one resource deny access to an unrelated resource for up to the 30s TTL (availability/incorrect-deny, not escalation, since only denials are stored). The key also omits group/resource, relying on `action` to encode them. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions or include explicit length/field delimiters.

The candidate adds examples and a secondary note about omitted fields, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Every non-allowed Check now hits the database; denial cache is per (name, folder) and unbounded

The cache lookups were removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (a real `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` query) whenever the cached scope map does not already allow the request. The only protection against repeated queries is `permDenialCache`, whose key includes the resource name and parent folder (cache.go:30) and whose TTL is only 30s. Consequently a caller that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (object-by-object checks, or a client enumerating names) produces one uncached DB permission query per unique (action, name, folder) tuple, and fills the shared local cache with one entry per tuple (the authlib local cache has no size bound), so both DB load and memory are driven by caller-controlled input. This amplification is worse in-proc because the client-side cache was also disabled (rbac.go:103). Consider keeping a bounded/short-lived "permissions were just fetched" marker per (user, action) so the full re-query happens at most once per short interval rather than once per resource.

Stale folder tree still causes denials, and those denials are now cached

`Check` now re-queries permissions from the DB when the cached scope map does not allow the request, but `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still returns the cached folder tree (30s TTL) and is never refreshed when the requested parent folder is absent from it. So for a resource whose access is granted only through inheritance from an ancestor (e.g. a dashboard created in a brand-new subfolder of a folder the user has permissions on), the tree does not yet contain the new folder, the check denies, and the denial is then stored in `permDenialCache` (line 154), extending the window during which the user cannot see the newly created object. The stated goal of the PR (immediate access to newly created folders/dashboards) is therefore only met for directly-granted scopes. Consider re-fetching the folder tree (or at least not caching the denial) when `req.ParentFolder` is not present in the cached tree.

permissionCacheUsage metric is mislabelled on the new Check paths

In `Check`, a denial-cache hit increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="true"}` (line 118) even though the permission cache was not consulted at all, conflating two different caches in one metric. Conversely, when the permission cache *is* hit but the result is "not allowed", execution continues and line 137 increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="false"}`, reporting a cache miss for a request that was served from the cache. Cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts built on this metric will be wrong after this change; the denial cache should get its own metric and the hit label should reflect whether `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeded.

Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID instead of the resolved user UID

`permDenialKey` uses `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw value parsed from the subject, while `permCache` keys use the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID` (see `getCachedIdentityPermissions`/`getUserPermissions`). Because `GetUserIdentifiers` treats a numeric subject as a user ID, the same identity addressed as `user:1` and as `user:<uid>` gets two independent denial entries (wasted lookups/queries), and a user whose UID is literally a decimal number shares denial entries with the user whose internal ID equals that number, which can deny the wrong identity for the TTL. Resolve the identifiers first and build the denial key from `userIdentifiers.UID` for consistency.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError and return a 500

The new check indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally. `sender` is only written by `build_integration` when the incoming state contains it (currently only the GitHub `installation` webhook path), so integrations created before that metadata existed, or by any flow where the webhook did not supply a sender, have no `sender` key. In that case the installation pipeline raises `KeyError` and the user gets an unhandled 500 instead of the intended "Invalid installation request." dialog. false_positives.candidate:
OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, so the new identity check can be bypassed

`OAuthLoginView` sends `state=pipeline.signature` to GitHub and then validates `request.GET["state"] == pipeline.signature` (line 412). `Pipeline.signature` is an md5 of the fully-qualified class names of the pipeline views, i.e. a value that is identical for every user and every session (the new test even hard-codes it as `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). It is therefore not a per-session nonce and provides no CSRF/session binding: an attacker who authorizes the GitHub OAuth app themselves can hand a victim a URL such as `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known_signature>`. The victim's pipeline will accept it, exchange the attacker's code, and bind `github_authenticated_user` to the attacker's login — which then matches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` and defeats exactly the installer-identity check this PR adds. Follow the existing pattern in `sentry.identity.oauth2` (`OAuth2LoginView` generates `secrets.token_hex()`, binds it with `pipeline.bind_state("state", ...)`, and `OAuth2CallbackView` compares it with `constant_time_compare`).

Installer-identity check is skipped when the Integration row does not yet exist

The comparison between `github_authenticated_user` and the installing GitHub user only happens in the branch where an `Integration` row already exists (lines 493-505). If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline immediately advances (line 482) and `build_integration` creates the integration with no identity validation at all. Since that row is created asynchronously by the GitHub `installation` webhook, an attacker who completes the Sentry pipeline before the webhook is processed (or on an instance where the webhook is not delivered) still gets the previous, unvalidated behaviour. Consider validating the authenticated user against the installation data returned by `get_installation_info()` (e.g. the account/sender) in that path as well, so the protection does not depend on a webhook race.

Unhandled exception from `get_user_info` / `safe_urlopen` yields a 500 instead of the error dialog

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` performs an HTTP call and raises on non-2xx responses (`raise_for_status`), and `safe_urlopen` on line 423 can raise on network/timeout errors. Neither is wrapped in a try/except, so a transient GitHub failure or a revoked/invalid token during installation surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the setup popup rather than the `github-integration-failed.html` dialog that the rest of this view carefully returns. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure (ideally with logging so these failures are diagnosable).

`test_installation_not_found` no longer tests installation-not-found

The test still stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{id}` but now passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, which does not match the pipeline signature used everywhere else in this file (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`). The request therefore fails in `OAuthLoginView` on the state check and the assertion only verifies the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The previously covered behaviour — `build_integration` raising `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` for a 404 from GitHub — is now untested, and nothing covers the missing-`access_token` or user-mismatch-in-OAuthLoginView branches separately. `client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated raw into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` comes from `absolute_uri(...)` and can contain characters that must be percent-encoded in a query value (e.g. when the install URL carries a query string or when a custom `SENTRY_URL_PREFIX`/subdomain introduces reserved characters), which would silently corrupt the redirect GitHub uses. Build the query with `urlencode({...})` as `OAuth2LoginView` does.

`_(error_short)` cannot be extracted for translation

`error()` calls `_(error_short)` on a runtime variable. The literal strings passed by callers ("Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion.", "Github installed on another Sentry organization.") are no longer wrapped in `_()` at their definition sites, so `makemessages` will not extract them and they will never be translated (the long messages are correctly marked, the short ones are not). Mark the short strings with `gettext_lazy` at the call sites and drop the runtime `_()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation decision uses the organization-aware (wrapped) model

`update()` obtains `idpById` from `getById(...)`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled) returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization is disabled or the realm's organization provider is disabled, regardless of the IDP's stored `enabled` flag. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate()` then evaluates `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` (which includes `isEnabled`) on this wrapper for `original` and on the raw REST model for `updated`. Consequence: when an org-linked IDP is edited while its organization (or the realm's organization support) is disabled, `test(original)` is false for org reasons and, if the update also makes `test(updated)` false (e.g. setting `broker.public=false` or `hideOnLogin=true`), the login caches are not invalidated at all. The cached ID list, however, was produced by the JPA query which ignores organization enablement, so it still contains that IDP; once the organization is re-enabled, `getForLogin` returns it and consumers only re-check `isEnabled()` (not `hideOnLogin`/`linkOnly`/`broker.public`), so a hidden or non-public broker can be rendered on the login page. The comparison should be done against the raw stored model (e.g. `idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId())`).

Login cache key omits organizationId, so one entry accumulates one search key per organization

`cacheKeyForLogin()` only includes the realm id and the `FetchMode`, and the organization id is used as the *search key* inside a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL` the organization id varies per login (see `OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean` which calls `getForLogin(ALL, organization.getId())`), so every distinct organization adds a new search key to the same cached object. Each first-time organization hits the `cached == null` branch, which calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` (a cluster-wide invalidation that wipes the login cache for that fetch mode on all nodes) and then rebuilds the query copying all previously cached search keys. With N organizations this is O(N^2) copying, one unboundedly growing cache entry per fetch mode, and continuous cluster-wide cache thrashing plus DB re-loads on all nodes. Including the organization id in the cache key (as `getByOrganization` does with `cacheKeyOrgId`) avoids both the growth and the repeated invalidations.

getLoginPredicate() now embeds organization semantics for all its callers

`LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` is public API in server-spi and is used outside the new invalidation logic (e.g. as the base of `IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate()`). Adding `idp.getOrganizationId() == null || Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` silently changes the result for every existing caller: any IDP that carries an organization id but no `broker.public=true` config is now considered not available for login. The test also only asserts the size of the cached id sets and never compares the stream actually returned by `getForLogin` against the uncached delegate result, so an incorrect set of ids or dropped entries would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. Adding a `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` check immediately after `Lock()` would make the initialization happen exactly once instead of once per concurrent request.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled as soon as the request completes

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which will normally happen before (or shortly after) the goroutine gets scheduled. The derived context is therefore already cancelled, so the legacy SQL store call will abort with `context canceled` and the 10s timeout is effectively meaningless. The whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, so this silently drops most legacy writes. The goroutine needs a context detached from the request lifetime (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying the requester/identity values) before applying the timeout.

Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

In the goroutines for Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into a duration histogram's `isError` label; nothing is logged. The previous implementation logged these failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, ...). With mode 3 this means legacy and unified storage can silently drift apart with no operator-visible signal other than an aggregate metric label, making divergence impossible to diagnose per object. Log the error together with the object name/kind.

Spawned goroutines have no panic recovery, so a legacy store panic kills the process

The four `go func()` blocks (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Panics inside an HTTP handler are recovered by the apiserver's panic middleware, but a panic in a detached goroutine terminates the entire Grafana process. Since these goroutines run arbitrary legacy storage code (including validation callbacks passed in from the request), a single bad object can now crash the server instead of failing one request. Add a recover (and log) wrapper around the goroutine bodies.

Update error path records a legacy duration for a storage failure

`d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is called when `d.Storage.Update` returns an error. As in Create, a unified-storage failure is recorded against the legacy backend's histogram and the storage histogram misses the failure entirely, producing misleading metrics. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Legacy Update is now driven by the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage

The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy received exactly the object that was persisted to unified storage. Now the unmodified `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy re-evaluates the update against the *legacy* copy of the object. For PATCH/apply requests the transformers are re-run against a different base object, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion the precondition is checked against the legacy resourceVersion (which is not the same value space as unified storage), so the legacy write can fail with a spurious conflict. Combined with the fact that the error is only counted in a metric, this silently diverges the two stores.

NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphaned legacy rows

The old Delete explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still issued the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. written before the mode switch, or whose unified write failed) can never be deleted: reads come from unified storage, so the row is invisible, and the delete never reaches legacy. Consider keeping the NotFound passthrough so legacy cleanup still happens.

Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write, and leak unsynchronized goroutines

The new tests use a single `mock.Mock` instance shared by `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so a call to legacy is indistinguishable from a call to storage, and no test asserts that the legacy store was written at all. The central behaviour of mode 3 (write to unified, then asynchronously mirror to legacy) is therefore untested; the mislabeled metrics and the context-cancellation problem in dualwriter_mode3.go would not be caught. In addition, nothing waits for the spawned goroutine, so the mock is invoked after the subtest finishes - any future assertion on legacy calls will be flaky, and an unmatched expectation would panic in a background goroutine and abort the whole test binary. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage and add synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) so the async write can be asserted deterministically.

Loki's `applyTemplateVariables` deliberately strips `__auto`/`__interval`/`__interval_ms`/`__range*` from `scopedVars` because those are interpolated on the backend, so in production `$__auto` will still be present in the expression after this new front-end interpolation step and will be resolved per sub-request range on the backend — i.e. the behaviour the linked issue complains about. With the current mock the assertion on `count_over_time({a="b"}[5m])` passes no matter what `applyTemplateVariables` does with `$__auto`, giving false confidence that the issue is fixed. The candidate describes this via the mocked replace() ignoring scopedVars, which is the same underlying concern as the unused third parameter.
